name: Gary Ridgway

victims.suspected: At least 71 (49 confirmed plus about 22 additional suspected)

victimProfile: Women and teenage girls, most of them sex workers or runaways picked up along Pacific Highway South in King County
captureMethod: DNA from a saliva sample police had collected from him in 1987 was matched to evidence recovered from three of the earliest victims.
sentence: 48 consecutive life sentences without parole (2003); a 49th consecutive life sentence (2011)
fateDetail: Washington State Penitentiary, Walla Walla
summary: Imprisoned. Gary Ridgway, the Green River Killer, pleaded guilty in 2003 to 48 murders of women and girls in King County, Washington, between 1982 and 1998, and to a 49th in 2011. He is serving 49 consecutive life sentences without parole.
narrative: Gary Leon Ridgway, known as the Green River Killer, is an American serial killer who murdered women and teenage girls in King County, Washington, between 1982 and 1998. He pleaded guilty in King County Superior Court on November 5, 2003, to 48 counts of aggravated first-degree murder, and on February 18, 2011, to a 49th. He is serving 49 consecutive life sentences without parole at the Washington State Penitentiary in Walla Walla. In taped interviews he claimed as many as 71 victims, and investigators continue to examine other cases as possibly connected.

The killings began in the summer of 1982. According to the victim list published by The Seattle Times when Ridgway entered his pleas, the first, Wendy Lee Coffield, 16, disappeared on July 8, 1982; her body was found in the Green River near Kent on July 15. Most of the 48 women and girls he admitted killing disappeared in 1982 and 1983 from the Pacific Highway South corridor between Seattle and Tacoma, where many were working as prostitutes or living as runaways. Ridgway strangled his victims, by hand or with a ligature, and left their bodies in wooded areas south and east of Seattle. Later admitted killings were sporadic: Patricia Barczak in 1986, Roberta Hayes in 1987, Marta Reeves in 1990 and Patricia Yellow Robe in 1998.

The King County Sheriff's Office formed the Green River Task Force in 1982, and Ridgway came to its attention early. The Associated Press reported that in 1983 the boyfriend of victim Marie Malvar told police he had seen her get into Ridgway's pickup; Ridgway denied knowing her and was cleared. In 1984 he contacted the task force himself, passed a polygraph examination and was cleared again. Police collected hair and saliva samples from him in April 1987, but DNA technology of the time could not produce a match.

The break came nearly two decades later. According to The Associated Press, advances in DNA analysis allowed the 1987 saliva sample to be matched to DNA recovered from the bodies of three of the earliest victims. Ridgway, then 52, was arrested on November 30, 2001, as he left his longtime job as a painter at the Kenworth truck plant in Renton.

Facing the death penalty, Ridgway signed a plea agreement with King County prosecutors on June 13, 2003. In exchange for his life, he agreed to confess, to help investigators find victims whose remains had never been located and to plead guilty to any future King County charge corroborated by reliable evidence. He led investigators to the remains of Pammy Avent, Marie Malvar and April Buttram. On November 5, 2003, he pleaded guilty to 48 counts of aggravated first-degree murder, four of them for victims known only as Jane Doe. On December 18, 2003, Judge Richard A. Jones sentenced him to 48 consecutive life terms without parole; The Seattle Times reported a $480,000 fine, $10,000 per victim, and 48 seconds of courtroom silence.

The agreement was invoked again in 2011. On December 21, 2010, teenagers found a skull in a ravine near Auburn that was identified as Rebecca Marrero, 20, last seen leaving a motel in 1982. Ridgway had confessed to killing her in 2003 but was not charged for lack of conclusive evidence. On February 18, 2011, he pleaded guilty to her murder in Kent, and Judge Mary E. Roberts imposed a 49th consecutive life sentence. In September 2024 Ridgway was briefly booked into the King County jail on an investigative hold; KOMO News reported the sheriff's office was still examining potentially related cases. In December 2025 the Department of Corrections denied reports that he was receiving end-of-life care.

Ridgway was born in Salt Lake City, Utah, on February 18, 1949, grew up in the SeaTac area and graduated from Tyee High School in 1969. He served in the U.S. Navy, including a deployment to Vietnam, was married three times, and worked for about three decades as a spray painter at the Kenworth plant before his arrest.

name: H. H. Holmes (Herman Webster Mudgett)

victims.suspected: About 9 (8 confirmed, 1 probable); claims of 27 to 200 or more are not supported by the record

victimProfile: Business associates, employees, lovers and their children, drawn into his insurance and property frauds; three victims were children aged 8 to 15
captureMethod: Arrested in Boston by Pinkerton detectives after the Fidelity Mutual Life Association, tipped by a fellow prisoner, questioned the staged death of Benjamin Pitezel.
sentence: Death; convicted by a Philadelphia jury of first-degree murder in the death of Benjamin F. Pitezel (1895), affirmed by the Pennsylvania Supreme Court on March 4, 1896
fateDetail: Hanged at Moyamensing Prison, Philadelphia, on May 7, 1896; buried at Holy Cross Cemetery, Yeadon, Pennsylvania; remains exhumed and identified in 2017
summary: Executed in 1896. Herman Webster Mudgett, alias H. H. Holmes, was convicted in Philadelphia of murdering Benjamin Pitezel and is tied to about nine deaths in Chicago, Indianapolis and Toronto. He confessed to 27, a figure the record does not support.
narrative: H. H. Holmes, born Herman Webster Mudgett, was a swindler and murderer active in Chicago, Philadelphia, Indianapolis and Toronto between 1891 and 1894. He was convicted of one murder, that of his business associate Benjamin F. Pitezel, by a Philadelphia jury in 1895. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court affirmed the first-degree murder verdict on March 4, 1896, and he was hanged at Moyamensing Prison on May 7, 1896. He confessed to 27 murders, but several people he named were later found alive, and historians count about nine confirmed or probable victims.

According to the Wikipedia article and Smithsonian magazine, the earliest confirmed victims were Julia Conner, who worked in Holmes's Englewood drugstore, and her daughter Pearl, last seen shortly before Christmas 1891. Emeline Cigrand disappeared in 1892 and the sisters Minnie and Nannie Williams in 1893. Smithsonian reported that most of his victims were people he had befriended or employed and whose deaths served his frauds.

The case that ended his career was an insurance fraud. According to the Pennsylvania Supreme Court opinion in Commonwealth v. Mudgett, Pitezel was insured for $10,000 with the Fidelity Mutual Life Association, and Holmes had arranged with him to fake his death. Instead, Pitezel's body was found on September 4, 1894, at 1316 Callowhill Street in Philadelphia, where he had been living as B. F. Perry. Medical witnesses testified that he died of chloroform poisoning that could not have been self-administered, and the prosecution argued that Holmes burned the body to make the death look accidental. Holmes identified the body and the insurer paid the claim.

Holmes then took custody of three Pitezel children. According to the Wikipedia article, Howard Pitezel was killed in Indianapolis on October 10, 1894, and Alice and Nellie Pitezel in Toronto on October 25, 1894. Holmes was arrested in Boston on November 17, 1894, after a Pinkerton pursuit; the article credits a convict, Marion Hedgepeth, with alerting the insurer. Smithsonian reported that Philadelphia detective Frank Geyer found the girls' bodies in a Toronto cellar in July 1895 and that charred remains of their brother were found at a cottage Holmes had rented in Indianapolis.

A Philadelphia grand jury indicted Holmes on September 12, 1895, and the trial opened on October 28, 1895. According to the Supreme Court opinion, Holmes dismissed his lawyers after jury selection had begun and conducted part of his own defense. The jury found him guilty of murder in the first degree. On appeal the court overruled all 13 assignments of error, held that he 'had a fair trial, and that is all he has a right to demand', and affirmed the judgment. Before his execution he sold the Hearst newspapers a confession claiming 27 murders; the Wikipedia article and historian Adam Selzer, writing in Time Out Chicago, note that some of those named were still alive. The Philadelphia Inquirer reported that he took more than 15 minutes to die on the gallows and was buried, at his request, in a concrete-filled coffin at Holy Cross Cemetery in Yeadon, Pennsylvania.

The 'Murder Castle' at 63rd Street and Wallace Avenue in Chicago is the most contested part of the story. Smithsonian and Time Out Chicago reported that Selzer's research found the first floor held shops, the second long-term apartments, and the unfinished third floor was never opened; the Chicago press described the hidden rooms in 1893 as places where Holmes concealed furniture bought on credit. Reports of torture chambers and a crematorium came from the yellow press of 1895 and were largely debunked at the time; the claim that he killed hundreds first appeared in 1930s pulp magazines. The building burned in August 1895 and was demolished in 1938.

In 2017 a Delaware County judge allowed the grave to be opened at a descendant's request. PhillyVoice and NBC Philadelphia reported that University of Pennsylvania Museum researchers recovered the remains, that dental records and DNA identified them as Holmes, and that they were reburied on August 30, 2017. Mudgett was born in Gilmanton, New Hampshire, on May 16, 1861, graduated from the University of Michigan medical program in June 1884, and moved to Chicago in 1886, where he adopted the Holmes name.

name: Henry Lee Lucas

victims.suspected: Disputed: a Texas task force once attributed 200 or more killings to him; the Texas Attorney General's 1986 report found most of his confessions false, and DNA later excluded him from at least one murder he was convicted of

victimProfile: No consistent profile; the murders he was convicted of include his mother, an elderly woman he was hired to care for, a child in his care, and women and girls aged 16 to 65 killed along Texas highways
captureMethod: Arrested in Montague County, Texas, in June 1983 on a firearm charge while under suspicion in the disappearances of Kate Rich and Becky Powell, after which he began confessing in custody
sentence: Death for the 1979 "Orange Socks" murder (1984), commuted to life in 1998; six other life sentences plus 210 years in Texas for nine more murders; up to 40 years in Michigan for killing his mother (1960)
fateDetail: Ellis Unit, Huntsville, Texas; found dead of apparent heart failure on March 12, 2001
summary: Died in prison in 2001. Texas drifter convicted of 11 murders who confessed to about 600 killings in 1983 to 1985 and then recanted; a 1986 Texas Attorney General report found most confessions false, and his death sentence was commuted in 1998.
narrative: Henry Lee Lucas was a drifter convicted of eleven murders: his mother in Michigan in 1960, a West Virginia patrolman, and nine killings in Texas between 1970 and 1983 (Wikipedia; Associated Press, 1998). He claimed roughly 600 murders in 1983 to 1985 before recanting almost all of them, and the Texas Attorney General concluded in 1986 that most of the confessions were false. His only death sentence, in the Williamson County "Orange Socks" case, was commuted to life by Governor George W. Bush in June 1998, and he died in a Texas prison in March 2001.

The first killing in the record was that of his mother, Viola Lucas, in Michigan on January 11, 1960. Lucas, then 23, stabbed her in the neck after an argument, claimed self-defense, and was convicted of second-degree murder and sentenced to up to 40 years; United Press International reported that he was released on June 3, 1970. On August 9, 1970, schoolteacher Linda Jane Phillips, 26, was abducted while driving home from a party near Richardson, Texas, and stabbed to death. Lucas pleaded guilty to that murder in Kaufman County in May 1984 and received a life term under a plea bargain.

By the late 1970s Lucas was travelling with Florida drifter Ottis Toole and later with Toole's young niece, Frieda "Becky" Powell. In 1982 Lucas and Powell were hired to care for Kate Rich, 82, of Ringgold, Texas. Powell disappeared in August 1982 and Rich in September. Lucas was arrested in Montague County in June 1983 on a firearm charge and soon told authorities he had killed both. In November 1983 he pleaded guilty to both murders. Neither body was ever positively identified.

His confessions then multiplied to roughly 600. The Texas Department of Public Safety set up a Lucas Task Force after confessions to 28 unsolved murders appeared to check out, and hundreds of homicides were marked cleared on his word; the Wikipedia article says at least 200 were attributed to him. He was given access to case files, which investigators later concluded shaped what he said.

The most consequential confession concerned an unidentified woman found strangled in a ditch off Interstate 35 in Williamson County on October 31, 1979, wearing only orange socks. A jury convicted Lucas of capital murder and he was sentenced to death in 1984, in a case the Fifth Circuit said rested "primarily, upon Lucas's confessions of guilt"; the state never identified the victim. His defense was that he was working a construction job in Jacksonville, Florida, that day; work records and a cashed paycheck supported the alibi, which the jury rejected.

In April 1985 the Dallas Times Herald showed that many confessions were physically impossible, and Lucas recanted. Attorney General Jim Mattox's April 1986 "Lucas Report" compared his claims with documented whereabouts, concluded he had falsely confessed to most of the murders, and suggested some agencies had cleared cases to close them. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals nonetheless affirmed the Orange Socks conviction in 1989, and on January 9, 1998 the Fifth Circuit held that a bare claim of actual innocence was not a ground for federal habeas relief and that the new evidence did not prove him innocent.

On June 26, 1998, days before a scheduled execution, Governor Bush accepted the Board of Pardons and Paroles' recommendation and commuted the sentence to life, saying serious concerns had been raised about his guilt, the Associated Press reported. He remained under six other life sentences and 210 years for nine further murders. He died at the Ellis Unit in Huntsville late on March 12, 2001, at 64, of apparent heart failure, ABC News reported. According to the Wikipedia article, the Orange Socks victim was identified as Debra Jackson, 23, in 2019.

In the 1983 Montgomery County murder of Laura Purchase, to which Lucas confessed and for which he was convicted in 1986, DNA testing in 2008 excluded both Lucas and Toole, and in May 2021 Thomas Elvin Darnell of Kansas was charged with capital murder after a genealogy-assisted DNA match, the AP and KPRC reported. Lucas was born on August 23, 1936, in Blacksburg, Virginia; the Wikipedia article describes a childhood of abuse and head injuries.

name: Herb Baumeister

victims.suspected: At least 11 at Fox Hollow Farm (coroner estimates up to 25 or more), plus 9 deaths in Indiana and Ohio from 1980 to 1990 linked by sheriffs in 1998

victimProfile: Men and teenage boys aged about 15 to 34, most of them gay men met at Indianapolis bars and a gay theater
captureMethod: Never arrested: a would-be victim recorded his licence plate in 1995, his wife consented to a search of Fox Hollow Farm in June 1996, and he died by suicide in Ontario before he could be questioned or charged.
fateDetail: Shot himself at Pinery Provincial Park, Ontario, Canada, on July 3, 1996, aged 49
summary: Died by suicide before charges. Indianapolis thrift-store owner whose Westfield estate, Fox Hollow Farm, yielded the remains of at least 11 men in 1996; sheriffs later linked him to nine more deaths along I-70. Identifications continue.
narrative: Herbert Richard Baumeister (1947 to 1996) was an Indianapolis businessman suspected of killing men at Fox Hollow Farm, his 18-acre estate in Westfield, Hamilton County, Indiana, in the mid-1990s, and of further killings in central Indiana and western Ohio between 1980 and 1990. He was never arrested, charged or tried. In June 1996 investigators recovered thousands of burned and crushed bone fragments from his property, representing at least 11 people; he fled to Canada and shot himself on July 3, 1996. The Hamilton County coroner has said the roughly 10,000 fragments could represent 25 or more victims, and identification work continued in 2025.

Per the Wikipedia article, Marion County and Indianapolis police began investigating the disappearances of gay men in the early 1990s. The men later tied to Fox Hollow Farm vanished between May 1993 and March 1995; the eight identified by 1999, as listed by WRTV, were Johnny Bayer, Allen Wayne Broussard, Roger Allen Goodlet, Richard D. Hamilton, Steven S. Hale, Jeff Allen Jones, Michael Keirn and Manuel Resendez. Police believed Baumeister met young men at gay bars, strangled them at home, then burned the bodies and scattered the crushed bones on the farm, WRTV reported.

The break came from a survivor. In 1994 Tony Harris told police that a man calling himself "Brian Smart" had tried to strangle him and, he believed, had killed his friend Roger Goodlet, according to the Wikipedia account. In August 1995 Harris saw the man again and recorded his licence plate, which led investigators to Baumeister. He and his wife initially refused a search. WRTV reported that his wife, Juliana, filed for divorce in January 1996 and told investigators that a child had found a human skull on the farm in December 1994, which Baumeister called a medical specimen from his late father, an anesthesiologist.

In June 1996, while Baumeister was away, his wife consented to a search. Investigators recovered bone fragments from at least 11 people; the Wikipedia article dates the recovery to June 24, 1996. A warrant was issued, but Baumeister drove to Ontario and shot himself at Pinery Provincial Park on July 3, 1996, aged 49. WRTV reported that his three-page note apologised for his failing marriage and businesses but did not mention the missing men. He died before any charge was filed, so no court ever ruled on his responsibility for the deaths.

United Press International reported on April 28, 1998, that sheriffs in Indiana and Ohio had linked nine further deaths to Baumeister: men aged 15 to 29, strangled between 1980 and 1990 and left in streams or culverts in Hancock, Hamilton and Shelby counties in Indiana and Darke and Preble counties in Ohio, all within 70 miles of the farm. A friend of 1983 victim Michael Riley identified Baumeister as the last man seen with Riley outside an Indianapolis gay theater, UPI reported. CBS News reported that by 1999 authorities had linked him to at least 16 disappearances since 1980.

The case was revived in 2022 when Hamilton County Coroner Jeff Jellison reopened the effort to name the remains, in storage for 26 years. On December 4, 2022, coroner's staff and cadaver dogs searched the property, found one more bone and flagged about 20 locations, WRTV reported. Jellison asked relatives of men missing from the mid-1980s to mid-1990s for DNA swabs; per CBS News, 44 bones went to the Indiana State Police laboratory and more than 30 families gave samples.

On October 17, 2023, Jellison announced that forensic genetic genealogy had identified Allen Lee Livingston, 27 when reported missing in August 1993, as the ninth presumed victim, CBS News reported. In January 2024 remains were matched to Manuel Resendez, missing since the same day as Livingston. On April 29, 2025, the coroner's office and Othram announced the identification of Daniel Thomas Halloran, born May 10, 1972, missing since 1994; ABC-affiliate reporting called him the tenth victim identified.

Baumeister was born in Indianapolis on April 7, 1947, the eldest of four children of an anesthesiologist. He married Juliana Saiter in November 1971; they had three children. Per the Wikipedia article, he bought Fox Hollow Farm in May 1988 and founded the Sav-A-Lot thrift stores the same year.

name: Israel Keyes
victimProfile: Strangers chosen at random, including a teenage barista in Anchorage and a married couple in their fifties in Vermont
captureMethod: Stopped by Texas Highway Patrol near Lufkin while driving a rental car matching a bulletin, after ransom money deposited into Samantha Koenig's account was tracked to ATM withdrawals in Alaska, New Mexico, Arizona and Texas.
fateDetail: Found dead in his cell at the Anchorage Correctional Complex on the morning of December 2, 2012, while awaiting a March 2013 federal trial
summary: Died before trial. Israel Keyes was indicted for the 2012 kidnapping and killing of Samantha Koenig in Anchorage, confessed to murdering Bill and Lorraine Currier in Vermont and five others, and died by suicide in custody in December 2012.
narrative: Israel Keyes was an Anchorage contractor and Army veteran indicted in federal court in April 2012 for the kidnapping and killing of 18-year-old Samantha Koenig. In custody he confessed to killing William and Lorraine Currier of Essex, Vermont, in June 2011. He was never convicted: he died by suicide in the Anchorage Correctional Complex in December 2012, about three months before trial. According to U.S. Attorney Karen Loeffler, quoted by the Anchorage Daily News, Keyes said he had killed Koenig, the Curriers and five others. In August 2013 the FBI said it had linked 11 killings to him based on his statements, most unnamed and unverified.

The Vermont State Police record that Bill Currier, 50, and Lorraine Currier, 55, were last seen at their Essex home on the evening of June 8, 2011, and that evidence at the house suggested they had not left voluntarily. According to the Anchorage Daily News, Keyes later said he had flown to Chicago, driven to Vermont, taken the couple in their own car to an abandoned farmhouse, shot Bill Currier and strangled Lorraine Currier. The farmhouse had been demolished before investigators arrived, and the bodies have not been located. Keyes was never charged in Vermont.

Samantha Koenig was abducted from the Common Grounds coffee stand in Anchorage on February 1, 2012. According to the account released by Anchorage police and the FBI in December 2012, reported by Alaska Public Media, Keyes approached in a ski mask near closing, bound her with zip ties and drove her to a shed at his home, where he sexually assaulted and strangled her. The next day he left on a pre-planned cruise from New Orleans. After returning on February 17 he photographed the body with a dated newspaper and left a typed $30,000 ransom demand in a city park. The remains were placed under the ice of Matanuska Lake; FBI divers recovered them in early April.

The ransom led to his arrest. The U.S. Attorney's Office stated that Koenig's family deposited reward money into the account linked to her stolen debit card so withdrawals could be tracked, and that Keyes withdrew money from ATMs in Alaska, New Mexico, Arizona and Texas. On March 13, 2012, a Texas Highway Patrol corporal stopped a white Ford Focus matching a bulletin near Lufkin, Texas; officers found Koenig's phone and ATM card. Returned to Alaska on a federal access-device fraud charge, the Anchorage Daily News reported, he soon confessed and told investigators where to find her body.

On April 18, 2012, the U.S. Attorney announced a federal grand jury indictment on three counts: kidnapping resulting in death, receiving and possessing ransom money, and access device fraud. The kidnapping count carried a maximum penalty of death or life imprisonment. Keyes pleaded not guilty to all three counts before U.S. District Judge Michael Thompson. In May 2012 he tried to escape by vaulting the courtroom rail and was subdued with a Taser. Trial was set for March 2013.

In FBI interviews Keyes described other killings. According to the Anchorage Daily News, he admitted to four murders in Washington state, where he lived from about 2001 to 2007, and one on the East Coast in 2009, with the body left in New York. He named none of those victims, and none has been identified. The FBI said he buried caches of weapons and body-disposal items, two of which were recovered in Alaska and New York, and that he financed his travel partly through bank robberies.

Keyes was found dead in his cell on the morning of December 2, 2012; Alaska State Troopers called it an apparent suicide, and Wikipedia gives the date of death as December 1. Because he died before trial, no court ever ruled on the Koenig charges or any other killing. In August 2013 the FBI released a timeline of his travels and said three further killings had been added based on his statements.

Keyes was born on January 7, 1978, in Richmond, Utah, according to Wikipedia. He served in the U.S. Army from 1998 to 2001, lived in Neah Bay, Washington, and moved to Anchorage in March 2007, where he ran a construction business and lived with his partner and daughter.

name: Jeffrey Dahmer
victimProfile: Men and boys aged 14 to 32, most of them Black, Hispanic or Asian, met at bars, malls and bus stops in Milwaukee
captureMethod: Tracy Edwards escaped Dahmer's Milwaukee apartment in handcuffs and flagged down police officers, who searched the apartment and found evidence of the killings.
sentence: 15 consecutive life terms in Wisconsin (February 17, 1992); a 16th consecutive life term without parole in Ohio (May 1, 1992)
fateDetail: Beaten to death by inmate Christopher Scarver at Columbia Correctional Institution, Portage, Wisconsin, November 28, 1994
summary: Died in prison. Jeffrey Dahmer murdered 17 men and boys in Ohio and Wisconsin between 1978 and 1991. A jury found him sane on 15 counts in 1992; he received 16 life terms and was killed by a fellow inmate in 1994.
narrative: Jeffrey Lionel Dahmer, known as the Milwaukee Cannibal, murdered 17 men and boys in Ohio and Wisconsin between 1978 and 1991 and was convicted of 16 of the killings. After he pleaded guilty but insane to 15 Wisconsin murders, a Milwaukee County jury found him sane on every count in February 1992 and he received 15 consecutive life terms; in May 1992 he pleaded guilty in Ohio to a 16th murder and received another life term. He was beaten to death by a fellow inmate at Columbia Correctional Institution in Portage, Wisconsin, on November 28, 1994.

According to the Wikipedia article, the first killing took place on June 18, 1978, three weeks after Dahmer's high school graduation, when he picked up an 18-year-old hitchhiker, Steven Hicks, and killed him at his family's home in Bath Township, Ohio. The second murder, of Steven Tuomi in a Milwaukee hotel room, came nine years later in 1987. Three further victims were killed at his grandmother's house in West Allis and twelve at the Oxford Apartments on North 25th Street in Milwaukee, where he moved in 1990. He met his victims, aged 14 to 32, at bars, malls and bus stops, offered them money to pose for photographs, and drugged and strangled them. In January 1989 he had pleaded guilty to second-degree sexual assault of a 13-year-old boy and served a work-release term followed by probation.

On May 27, 1991, Milwaukee police officers found 14-year-old Konerak Sinthasomphone, the older brother of the 1989 case's victim, naked and disoriented outside Dahmer's building. Dahmer told them the boy was his adult boyfriend, and the officers returned him to the apartment, where he was killed that day. Wikipedia, citing the federal district court's opinion in Estate of Sinthasomphone v. City of Milwaukee, notes that the family's civil claims against the city and officers were dismissed.

The killings ended on July 22, 1991, when Tracy Edwards, who had been handcuffed in the apartment, escaped and flagged down two patrol officers. They searched the apartment, found evidence of the murders and arrested Dahmer, who confessed to 17 killings over more than 60 hours of interviews, according to Wikipedia. He was charged with four counts of first-degree murder on July 25, 1991, and eleven more by August 22. UPI reported that Summit County prosecutors charged him in September 1991 with aggravated murder in the Hicks case.

Dahmer pleaded guilty but insane to the 15 Wisconsin counts on January 13, 1992, so the trial that began January 30 before Judge Laurence C. Gram Jr. concerned only his sanity. On February 15, 1992, the jury found him sane on each count, with two of twelve jurors dissenting. On February 17 Gram imposed mandatory life plus ten years on the first two counts and consecutive life terms on the other thirteen; Wisconsin has no death penalty. UPI and the Deseret News quoted Dahmer telling the court, "I hope that God can forgive me." On May 1, 1992, in Summit County Common Pleas Court in Akron, he pleaded guilty to the aggravated murder of Steven Hicks and was sentenced to life without parole, consecutive to the Wisconsin terms, UPI reported.

Dahmer was held at Columbia Correctional Institution in Portage, where UPI reported in July 1992 that he was in administrative confinement with a daily cleaning detail. On November 28, 1994, while cleaning a bathroom on a work detail, he was beaten by inmate Christopher Scarver, 25, and died on the way to hospital, UPI reported; inmate Jesse Anderson, attacked at the same time, died two days later. Scarver received two additional life terms in May 1995. In June 1995 a Wisconsin Department of Corrections panel found that Scarver had acted alone after a lapse in supervision, and four staff members were suspended, the Spokesman-Review reported.

The Oxford Apartments were demolished in November 1992, and a civic group bought and destroyed Dahmer's possessions. His remains were cremated in 1995. Dahmer was born in Milwaukee on May 21, 1960, and grew up in Bath Township, Ohio. He briefly attended Ohio State University, served in the Army in West Germany, and later lived with his grandmother in West Allis before renting the Milwaukee apartment.

name: Jerry Brudos
victimProfile: Young women aged 19 to 23, abducted from parking areas, a shopping center, a roadside and a door-to-door sales call in the Salem and Portland areas
captureMethod: Identified after an Oregon State University student he had phoned reported his call to police, then confirmed through a search warrant on his home and his confession
sentence: Three consecutive life terms with the possibility of parole, on guilty pleas to three counts of first-degree murder (Marion County Circuit Court, June 27, 1969); affirmed on appeal in 1970
fateDetail: Oregon State Penitentiary, Salem; died of liver cancer after nearly 37 years in custody
summary: Convicted on guilty pleas to three first-degree murders in Oregon in 1969 and sentenced to three consecutive life terms. Jerry Brudos confessed to four killings of young women in 1968 and 1969 and died in the Oregon State Penitentiary in 2006.
narrative: Jerome Henry Brudos, known as Jerry Brudos, pleaded guilty in June 1969 to three counts of first-degree murder for the killings of young women in the Salem and Portland areas of Oregon in 1968 and 1969. According to the Oregon Court of Appeals in State v. Brudos (1970), he entered the pleas orally and in writing with the advice of counsel and received three consecutive life sentences. Police attributed four murders to him and he admitted all four, but he was never tried for the fourth because the victim's body was not recovered. He died in the Oregon State Penitentiary in 2006.

According to the Wikipedia article and Biography.com, the first victim was Linda Slawson, a 19-year-old encyclopedia saleswoman from Aloha, who called at Brudos's home in the Portland area on January 26, 1968, and was killed there; her body was never found. On November 26, 1968, Jan Whitney, 23, disappeared after her car broke down on Interstate 5 between Salem and Albany. Brudos later admitted stopping for her and strangling her in his car. Her remains were recovered from the Willamette River near Independence after his conviction and identified by dental records.

Karen Sprinker, an 18-year-old Oregon State University student, was abducted at gunpoint from a department store parking garage in downtown Salem on March 27, 1969. Linda Salee, 22, of Beaverton, was taken from the Lloyd Center shopping area in Portland on April 23, 1969. In May 1969 both bodies were found in the Long Tom River, weighted with automobile parts and bound with cord. In the same week as the Salee abduction, two other young women escaped attempted abductions in Portland; one later identified Brudos.

Investigators noticed that the knots on both river victims matched and, because Sprinker was an OSU student, interviewed women on the Corvallis campus. One student reported that a caller had asked her for a date, and police asked her to report any further contact. When Brudos called again, officers were present at the meeting. According to the Wikipedia article, his home was searched under warrant on May 26, 1969, yielding nylon rope and photographs of the victims, and Oregon state troopers took him into custody on May 29 after finding him hiding in the family station wagon. In early June he confessed to the four murders and to earlier assaults.

Brudos was arraigned on June 4, 1969, in Marion County and initially pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity. Court-appointed psychiatrists found him legally sane. On June 27, 1969, before Circuit Judge Val D. Sloper, he pleaded guilty to the first-degree murders of Sprinker, Whitney and Salee and was sentenced to three consecutive life terms with the possibility of parole. His wife, Ralphene Brudos, was indicted in August 1969 in connection with the Sprinker murder and was acquitted at trial.

The Oregon Court of Appeals affirmed the convictions and sentences on July 9, 1970, holding that consecutive life terms were permissible and that any challenge to the pleas had to be raised through post-conviction relief; the Oregon Supreme Court denied review that September. Brudos then sought post-conviction relief, arguing his pleas were not knowing and voluntary. According to Brudos v. Cupp (1977), the post-conviction court rejected that claim and the Court of Appeals upheld the denial of his request to move the hearing out of Marion County. The Wikipedia article reports that later appeals failed and parole was repeatedly denied over the objections of the victims' families.

Brudos spent nearly 37 years at the Oregon State Penitentiary in Salem, where he held clerical jobs. He died there of liver cancer on March 28, 2006, at age 67, described by state officials as the longest-held inmate in the Oregon prison system.

Brudos was born on January 31, 1939, in Webster, South Dakota, and grew up in Oregon. According to the Wikipedia article, he was arrested in 1956 at age 17 for assaulting a girl and spent nine months under psychiatric evaluation at the Oregon State Hospital, graduated from Corvallis High School in 1957, was discharged from the Army in 1959 and married in 1961. He was living in Salem with his wife and two children at the time of the 1969 murders.

name: Joel Rifkin
victimProfile: Women aged roughly 21 to 41, most of them sex workers picked up in Manhattan
captureMethod: Stopped by state troopers for a missing rear license plate, fled, crashed, and was found with a victim's body in his pickup truck
sentence: Aggregate 203 years to life: 25 years to life by jury verdict in Nassau County (1994) plus consecutive terms on guilty pleas in Suffolk, Kings, Bronx and Queens counties (1995 to 1996)
fateDetail: Clinton Correctional Facility, Dannemora, New York
summary: Imprisoned. Joel Rifkin, a Long Island landscaper, confessed to killing 17 women in New York between 1989 and 1993 and was convicted of nine murders after a 1993 traffic stop revealed a body in his truck.
narrative: Joel David Rifkin is a convicted serial killer who murdered women in New York City and on Long Island between 1989 and 1993. According to the New York State Police, he admitted to 16 murders beyond the one for which he was arrested, 17 in all. He was convicted of nine murders in jury and plea proceedings in Nassau, Suffolk, Kings, Bronx and Queens counties between 1994 and 1996 and, according to NBC News, is serving an aggregate sentence of 203 years. He is held at Clinton Correctional Facility.

The known victims were women, most of them sex workers picked up in Manhattan, who were strangled after sexual encounters and whose bodies were left in waterways, wooded areas and other sites around the region. According to the Wikipedia article, the first killing was that of Heidi Balch, 25, in early 1989; a head found at a Hopewell Township, New Jersey golf course in March 1989 was identified as hers only in 2013. Other bodies were recovered from New York City rivers and creeks, upstate New York and Long Island between 1991 and 1993. Two victims were never found, and a woman found in a drum in Newtown Creek in May 1992 has never been identified.

The series ended with a traffic stop. According to the New York State Police, at about 3:15 a.m. on June 28, 1993, troopers Deborah Spaargaren and Sean Ruane tried to pull over a 1984 Mazda pickup on the Southern State Parkway because it had no rear plate. The driver fled at up to 90 mph, struck a light pole on Old Country Road after a 20 to 25 minute chase and was taken into custody. An inventory search of the truck found the body of Tiffany Bresciani, 22, who had disappeared four days earlier. At the station house Rifkin admitted to 16 further killings; a task force recovered the remains of 15 victims across 10 jurisdictions.

Rifkin was tried first in Nassau County for Bresciani's murder and raised an insanity defense. According to United Press International, on May 9, 1994 a jury deliberated just over two hours before convicting him of second-degree murder and first-degree reckless endangerment arising from the chase. Judge Ira Wexner sentenced him on June 8, 1994; wire reports described the combined term as 27 years to life. In December 2001 the Appellate Division, Second Department, held that statements Rifkin made at the crash scene after being handcuffed should have been suppressed because they preceded Miranda warnings, but affirmed the conviction in light of the otherwise overwhelming evidence, finding the later station-house confession voluntary.

The other convictions came by plea. In Suffolk County he admitted murdering Leah Evens and Lauren Marquez, both 28, and on September 18, 1995 Judge John Jones imposed two consecutive terms of 25 years to life, according to wire reports in The Spokesman-Review. In Brooklyn he pleaded guilty on December 1, 1995 to three counts of second-degree murder for Lorraine Orvieto, Mary Ann Holloman and an unidentified woman; UPI reported that on December 12 he received life with a 75-year minimum, consecutive to his earlier terms. According to Wikipedia, a further life sentence followed in January 1996 in the Bronx for the murder of Jenny Soto.

On January 25, 1996, Queens Supreme Court Justice Robert Hanophy added 25 years for the murder of Iris Sanchez, 25, whose body had been found under mattresses near Kennedy Airport. UPI reported that Rifkin, who by then had accumulated 177 years for seven murders, apologized to the victims' families and called himself a monster; the judge noted he was not eligible for New York's newly restored death penalty. In March 2013 Hopewell Township police announced that the 1989 remains had been identified through DNA from the victim's mother as Heidi Balch; NBC News reported that Rifkin would not be charged in New Jersey.

Rifkin was born in New York City on January 20, 1959, and was adopted as an infant by Bernard and Jeanne Rifkin of East Meadow, Long Island, according to Wikipedia. He graduated from East Meadow High School in 1977, attended several colleges without earning a degree and worked as a self-employed landscaper. He was 34 when arrested.

captureMethod: Des Plaines police investigating the disappearance of 15-year-old Robert Piest traced him to Gacy, who confessed after a search of his home turned up evidence tied to Piest.

summary: Executed in 1994. John Wayne Gacy was convicted by a Cook County jury in 1980 of murdering 33 boys and young men in suburban Chicago between 1972 and 1978; 29 were found at his home. Five victims remain unidentified.
narrative: John Wayne Gacy was a Chicago-area building contractor who murdered boys and young men at his home in Norwood Park Township, Cook County, Illinois, between 1972 and 1978. According to the Illinois Supreme Court's 1984 opinion in People v. Gacy, a Cook County jury convicted him of 33 counts of murder, one count of deviate sexual assault and one count of indecent liberties with a child, and sentenced him to death on 12 murder counts and to natural life on the rest. Illinois executed him on May 10, 1994. The opinion recites that his confession put the number at about 30; police recovered 33 bodies. Three of the eight victims buried unidentified have been named since the Cook County Sheriff's Office reopened the identification effort in 2011, and five remain unidentified.

The first known victim, Timothy McCoy, was killed on January 3, 1972, according to the victim list in the Wikipedia article. Over the next six years Gacy brought young men to the house, many of them employees or job applicants at his remodelling company, runaways or hitchhikers. NBC Chicago, in a 40th-anniversary report, described a handcuff and rope trick used to restrain and then strangle the victims, who ranged in age from 14 to 21. Twenty-six bodies were buried in the crawl space under the house, three elsewhere on the property, and four were thrown into the Des Plaines River.

The case broke on December 11, 1978, when 15-year-old Robert Piest left the Des Plaines pharmacy where he worked to talk to a contractor about a summer job and never returned. The Illinois Supreme Court opinion records that Gacy had been at the pharmacy that evening, that his truck was seen outside, and that police learned of his Iowa conviction for assaulting a teenage boy. Investigators obtained a search warrant for his home and vehicles on December 13, kept him under surveillance, and arrested him on December 21, 1978. Early on December 22 he confessed, saying bodies were buried under the house and five had been thrown into the river. Excavation recovered 29 bodies from the property; four more were pulled from the Des Plaines and Illinois rivers.

The trial opened on February 6, 1980, before Judge Louis Garippo with a jury drawn from Rockford. The defence argued insanity; the State's experts said Gacy had a personality disorder and was legally responsible. On March 12, 1980, after under two hours of deliberation, the jury found him guilty of all 33 murders. At sentencing the jury returned death sentences for the 12 murders committed after Illinois's 1977 death penalty statute took effect, and the court imposed natural life for the other 21.

The Illinois Supreme Court affirmed the convictions and sentences on June 6, 1984, rejecting challenges to the search warrants, jury selection and the insanity verdict, and the U.S. Supreme Court denied review in 1985. The Illinois Supreme Court upheld the dismissal of a post-conviction petition on September 29, 1988, and the Seventh Circuit, in Gacy v. Welborn on April 12, 1993, affirmed the denial of federal habeas relief. After 14 years on death row at Menard, Gacy was executed by lethal injection at Stateville Correctional Center shortly after midnight on May 10, 1994.

Eight victims were buried without names. In 2011 Cook County Sheriff Tom Dart had the remains exhumed and asked families of young men who vanished in the Chicago area in the 1970s to submit DNA. William Bundy, 19, was identified in November 2011. James Byron Haakenson, a 16-year-old runaway from Minnesota, was identified through a sister's DNA in July 2017, CBS Minnesota reported. On October 25, 2021, the sheriff's office announced that Victim No. 5 was Francis Wayne Alexander, a North Carolina native killed between early 1976 and early 1977 and identified through genetic genealogy with the DNA Doe Project, according to CBS News and ABC7. Five victims remain unidentified.

Gacy was born in Chicago on March 17, 1942. In 1968 he was convicted in Waterloo, Iowa, of sodomy involving a teenage boy; paroled on June 18, 1970, he returned to the Chicago area, ran a contracting business, was active in local Democratic politics and performed at events as a clown called Pogo.

summary: Imprisoned for life. Joseph DeAngelo, the Golden State Killer, pleaded guilty in 2020 to 13 California murders committed from 1975 to 1986 and admitted dozens of rapes; he was identified in 2018 through forensic genetic genealogy.
narrative: Joseph James DeAngelo is the former California police officer identified in 2018 as the Golden State Killer, the offender earlier known as the Visalia Ransacker, the East Area Rapist and the Original Night Stalker. On June 29, 2020, he pleaded guilty in Sacramento County Superior Court to 13 counts of first-degree murder with special circumstances and 13 counts of kidnapping, and under the plea he admitted dozens of uncharged rapes. NBC News reported that prosecutors described crimes against 87 victims at 53 crime scenes in 11 California counties between 1975 and 1986. On August 21, 2020, Judge Michael Bowman sentenced him to consecutive life terms without the possibility of parole.

The first killing DeAngelo admitted was the September 11, 1975 shooting of Claude Snelling in Visalia, Tulare County, during the period when the Visalia Ransacker was burglarizing homes there. According to the Wikipedia article, the East Area Rapist home-invasion attacks began in Rancho Cordova, near Sacramento, on June 18, 1976, and continued into 1979; Brian and Katie Maggiore were shot to death in Rancho Cordova on February 2, 1978. The attacks then moved to Southern California. According to the Wikipedia article and charges reported by NBC News, Robert Offerman and Debra Manning were killed in Goleta on December 30, 1979; Lyman and Charlene Smith in Ventura on March 13, 1980; Keith and Patrice Harrington in Dana Point on August 19, 1980; Manuela Witthuhn in Irvine on February 6, 1981; Cheri Domingo and Gregory Sanchez in Goleta on July 27, 1981; and Janelle Cruz in Irvine in May 1986. The later victims were bludgeoned in their homes after being bound.

DNA testing eventually linked the Southern California murders to the East Area Rapist attacks. In 2018 investigators uploaded a DNA profile from crime-scene evidence to the public genealogy database GEDmatch, built family trees from distant relatives who matched, and narrowed the candidates to DeAngelo. NBC News reported that Sacramento County Sheriff Scott Jones said investigators confirmed the match with discarded DNA after six days of surveillance; according to the Wikipedia article the samples came from his car door handle and a tissue in his trash. He was arrested at his Citrus Heights home on April 24, 2018, at age 72, in the first widely publicized arrest made through forensic genetic genealogy.

NBC News reported that at an August 2018 arraignment DeAngelo faced 13 murder counts across Sacramento, Santa Barbara, Tulare, Ventura and Orange counties and 13 kidnapping counts in Sacramento and Contra Costa counties; the kidnapping charges were used because California's statute of limitations barred prosecution of the rapes themselves. The district attorneys agreed to consolidate all of the cases in Sacramento.

The 2020 plea agreement spared DeAngelo the death penalty. The Associated Press, in a report carried by PBS NewsHour, said prosecutors had initially sought death but accepted life terms, citing California's execution moratorium, the pandemic and the ages of the defendant, victims and witnesses. Sentencing followed three days of victim impact statements in a university ballroom. DeAngelo, then 74, rose from a wheelchair and told the court he was sorry to everyone he had hurt, ABC News reported. The AP reported that Judge Bowman imposed 11 consecutive life terms without parole on the murder counts, additional life terms on the remaining counts and eight years for enhancements. He waived his right to appeal.

According to the Wikipedia article, DeAngelo is held in protective custody at California State Prison, Corcoran, and DNA testing has excluded him from several other unsolved killings once speculatively linked to the case.

DeAngelo was born on November 8, 1945, in Bath, New York, according to the Wikipedia article. He served in the Navy during the Vietnam War, studied police science and criminal justice, and worked as a police officer in Exeter from 1973 to 1976 and in Auburn from 1976 to 1979. NBC News reported that he was fired from the Auburn department in 1979 after being arrested for shoplifting a hammer and dog repellent. He raised three daughters in Citrus Heights and later worked as a truck mechanic. His wife filed for divorce after his arrest.

name: Kenneth Bianchi

victimProfile: Girls and young women aged 12 to 28 in Los Angeles, lured by the cousins posing as police officers; two university students aged 22 and 27 in Bellingham
captureMethod: Taken into custody by Bellingham police the day after two students he had hired to watch a house were found strangled; a note in the victim's car and his security job pointed to him, and jewelry and fiber evidence then tied him to the Los Angeles killings

summary: Imprisoned for life. Kenneth Bianchi, one of the two Hillside Stranglers, pleaded guilty in 1979 to five Los Angeles murders and two Bellingham, Washington murders; his cousin Angelo Buono was convicted of nine killings in 1983.
narrative: Kenneth Alessio Bianchi is one of the two Hillside Stranglers who, with his cousin Angelo Buono Jr., murdered girls and young women in the Los Angeles area between October 1977 and February 1978. He then killed two university students alone in Bellingham, Washington, in January 1979. In October 1979 he pleaded guilty in Washington to two counts of first-degree murder and in Los Angeles to five murders, conspiracy and sodomy. Courts have convicted him of seven murders; he confessed to those seven; police attribute twelve killings to the Hillside Strangler cases. He is serving life sentences at the Washington State Penitentiary in Walla Walla.

According to UPI and the Wikipedia article, Bianchi and Buono posed as police officers to lure victims, took them to Buono's upholstery shop in Glendale, strangled them and left the bodies on hillsides around Los Angeles. The ten Los Angeles victims named in the Wikipedia article were Yolanda Washington, 19; Judith Miller, 15; Lissa Kastin, 21; Jane King, 28; Dolores Cepeda, 12; Sonja Johnson, 14; Kristina Weckler, 20; Lauren Wagner, 18; Kimberly Martin, 17; and Cindy Hudspeth, 20. The first body was found on October 17, 1977, and the last on February 17, 1978.

According to HistoryLink, Bianchi was working for a Bellingham security company when, on January 11, 1979, he offered Western Washington University students Karen Mandic, 22, and Diane Wilder, 27, money to watch a house he was guarding. Both were found strangled in Mandic's car on January 12, 1979. A note in the car naming the house and "Ken" led Bellingham police to take him into custody that day. HistoryLink reports that jewelry in his home resembled items worn by Los Angeles victims, that FBI laboratory work matched fibers and hair to the house and to Bianchi, and that a Los Angeles task force detective recognized his name on January 13.

Charged on January 26, 1979, Bianchi pleaded not guilty and then, on March 30, 1979, not guilty by reason of insanity, claiming under hypnosis that a second personality named Steve had committed the crimes. According to the Wikipedia article, psychiatrist Martin Orne concluded he was simulating, and Bianchi later admitted faking the disorder. After being found competent, HistoryLink reports, he pleaded guilty on October 19, 1979, to both Bellingham murders under an agreement in which the prosecutor withdrew the death penalty request and Bianchi agreed to testify against Buono; Judge Jack Kurtz imposed two consecutive life terms. On October 22, 1979, in Los Angeles, he pleaded guilty to five Hillside Strangler murders, conspiracy to commit murder and sodomy, receiving concurrent life terms.

Buono was arrested in October 1979, and his trial became the longest criminal trial in United States history to that point. UPI reported that Bianchi testified for 80 days but that Judge Ronald George found he had not testified truthfully and completely, and ordered him to serve his sentence in Washington rather than California. A jury convicted Buono in November 1983 of nine of the ten Los Angeles murders; in January 1984 he received nine concurrent terms of life without parole. Bianchi was moved to Walla Walla on January 10, 1984. Buono died at Calipatria State Prison on September 21, 2002, according to the Wikipedia article and AP reporting cited by CBS News.

HistoryLink reports that in July 1990 the Washington parole board set Bianchi's minimum term at 116.5 years, with eligibility in 2059. CBS News, citing the Associated Press, reported that a California board denied him parole on August 18, 2010. The Los Angeles Times reported that the California Board of Parole Hearings denied parole again on July 10, 2025 with eligibility again in ten years, and that he maintains in appeals that his confession and pleas were coerced through hypnosis. Fox News reported that he changed his name to Anthony D'Amato in 2023 and that a Washington parole review was pending in July 2025.

Bianchi was born on May 22, 1951, in Rochester, New York, and was adopted as an infant. According to the Wikipedia article, he was a suspect but never charged in the 1971 to 1973 Rochester Alphabet murders, which he denies, and moved to Los Angeles in 1976 to live near Buono.

fateDetail: Lethal injection, Huntsville Unit, Texas, November 17, 1998
summary: Executed 1998. Texas killer sentenced to death for three 1966 murders, released on parole in 1989 after his sentence was commuted, and convicted of two 1991 to 1992 murders; his case drove Texas parole reform.
narrative: Kenneth Allen McDuff was a Texas murderer whose two killing periods, 1966 and 1989 to 1992, were separated by a death sentence, a commutation and a parole. Courts convicted him of five murders: three teenagers killed near Fort Worth in 1966, and Colleen Reed and Melissa Northrup, killed in 1991 and 1992. Texas executed him on November 17, 1998. Wikipedia's summary of the reporting puts the attributed toll at nine to fourteen or more. According to the University of North Texas Press, anger that a condemned man had been freed to kill again produced parole reforms and prison construction known collectively as the "McDuff Rules."

The 1966 crimes appear in testimony recited by the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. Roy Dale Green testified that on August 6, 1966, McDuff locked two teenage boys and a girl in the trunk of a parked car, shot the boys through the trunk, raped the girl and choked her with a broomstick; Green later turned him in. Wikipedia names the victims as Robert Brand, 17, Mark Dunnam, 15, and Edna Louise Sullivan, 16, abducted at Everman. McDuff was convicted of murder with malice and sentenced to death. After the Supreme Court's 1972 Furman v. Georgia decision the sentence became life imprisonment. The board paroled him in October 1989. Wikipedia also lists four deaths attributed to him after release for which he was never charged: Sarafia Parker in Temple in October 1989; Brenda Thompson and Regenia Moore, who vanished near Waco in October 1991 and whose remains were found in 1998; and Valencia Joshua, found in Waco in March 1992.

The two capital cases are described in court opinions. The Texas Court of Appeals in Austin recorded that Colleen Reed was abducted from an Austin car wash in late December 1991 and that her body had not been found at trial. The Fifth Circuit summarized the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals' findings on Melissa Northrup: around 4 a.m. on March 1, 1992, she was taken from the Waco Quik Pak where she worked and where McDuff had briefly been employed; a witness saw him driving her car with a frightened woman beside him; and her bound body was later found in a water-filled gravel pit. State experts linked hairs on her body and in her car to him.

McDuff abandoned his car in Waco and fled to Kansas City, Missouri, where, the Austin court noted, he lived under an alias from March 1992 and was arrested in May 1992 using a false name. Wikipedia reports that a co-worker recognized him from a May 1, 1992 America's Most Wanted broadcast and that he was arrested on May 4, 1992.

A McLennan County jury convicted McDuff of Northrup's capital murder and, according to Wikipedia, returned a death sentence on February 18, 1993. The Reed indictment, returned in Travis County, was tried in Guadalupe County after a change of venue. The Austin court recorded that the jury convicted him of capital murder, aggravated kidnapping and aggravated sexual assault, imposing death on the capital count and life terms on the others. The Court of Criminal Appeals affirmed the Reed death sentence in 1997; the Austin court that year reversed the sexual-assault count because the only witness was the accomplice, Alva Hank Worley, and affirmed the kidnapping count.

The Court of Criminal Appeals affirmed the Northrup conviction in 1997, the Supreme Court denied certiorari in 1998, and state and federal habeas relief were denied. On November 17, 1998, the Fifth Circuit refused a certificate of appealability, rejecting claims that the hair testimony was false and that another man was the killer. McDuff was executed by lethal injection at the Huntsville Unit that evening, aged 52. The Texas Department of Criminal Justice records his last statement as "I'm ready to be released. Release me." Wikipedia and Spectrum News report that in his final weeks he led investigators to Reed's remains.
McDuff was born on March 21, 1946, in Rosebud, Texas. Wikipedia records that in 1964 he was convicted of twelve burglary counts and paroled in December 1965, eight months before the Everman killings.

summary: Died in prison. Larry Eyler was convicted in Illinois in 1986 of murdering Daniel Bridges and sentenced to death, pleaded guilty in Indiana in 1990 to a second murder, and confessed through his attorney to 21 killings of young men in Illinois and Indiana between 1982 and 1984.
narrative: Larry William Eyler, called the Highway Killer or Interstate Killer, was a house painter who divided his time between Chicago and Terre Haute, Indiana. Between late 1982 and 1984 the bodies of teenage boys and young men were found near highways in Illinois and Indiana. A Cook County jury convicted him in 1986 of the murder of Daniel Bridges in Chicago and he was sentenced to death; he pleaded guilty in Indiana in 1990 to the 1982 murder of Steven Agan; and, in a statement his attorney released after his death, he confessed to 21 killings. He died of AIDS-related complications on death row in March 1994.

United Press International reported in October 1983 that a multi-agency task force was investigating at least 19 similar killings in Illinois and northern Indiana. Victims were typically restrained and stabbed and left in fields or woods near interstate exits. Ralph Calise, 28, of Chicago, was found in a cornfield near Lake Forest, Illinois, on August 31, 1983. By August 1984 UPI reported that police considered Eyler a suspect in as many as 24 slayings in four states.

Indiana State Police stopped Eyler on September 30, 1983, near Lowell, Indiana, and seized items from his truck. On October 28, 1983, Lake County, Illinois, authorities charged him with Calise's murder and held him on $1 million bond. In February 1984 Lake County Circuit Judge William Block ruled that Indiana police had detained Eyler illegally and seized his property without probable cause; the evidence was suppressed, bond was cut to $10,000 and Eyler was released on February 6, 1984, with the charge still pending.

According to the Illinois Supreme Court's 1989 opinion in People v. Eyler, the dismembered body of Danny Bridges, a 15-year-old who worked as a street prostitute in Chicago, was found in eight garbage bags in a dumpster on August 21, 1984. UPI reported that the dumpster stood outside Eyler's apartment building and that a janitor had seen Eyler put bags into it the previous afternoon. Eyler, still free on bond in the Calise case, was arrested that day and charged with murder and concealment of a homicidal death on August 22, 1984.

UPI reported that after about three hours of deliberation a Cook County jury on July 9, 1986, found Eyler guilty of murder committed during a kidnapping and aggravated kidnapping, making him eligible for the death penalty. Eyler waived a jury for the penalty phase and Judge Joseph Urso sentenced him to death on October 3, 1986, with additional terms for aggravated kidnapping and concealment. The Illinois Supreme Court affirmed the convictions and the death sentence on October 25, 1989.

In December 1990 Eyler gave Indiana investigators a statement about the December 1982 killing of Steven Agan, 23, a car-wash worker from Terre Haute. He pleaded guilty to Agan's murder in Vermillion County, Indiana, on December 13, 1990, and was sentenced to 60 years on December 28, 1990. He named Robert David Little, a former Indiana State University professor he had lived with, as a participant and testified against him; a Vermillion County jury acquitted Little on April 17, 1991. Newsweek reported in early 1991 that Eyler, through attorney Kathleen Zellner, offered to confess to as many as 20 further killings in exchange for a life sentence; Cook County State's Attorney Jack O'Malley declined.

Eyler died at Pontiac Correctional Center on March 6, 1994, at age 41. Two days later Zellner announced that he had confessed to killing 21 men and boys in Illinois and Indiana between 1982 and 1984, with an accomplice in four, while still denying that he killed Bridges. The Associated Press reported that a Cook County prosecutor's spokesman cautioned that the confessions did not prove Eyler committed the crimes. The AP reported in July 2023 that DNA genealogy identified Keith Lavell Bibbs, 16, of Chicago, found buried at a farm in Lake Village, Indiana, in 1983, as a victim Eyler had confessed to killing.
Eyler was born on December 21, 1952, in Crawfordsville, Indiana. Before his arrest he worked as a house painter and, briefly in 1984, at a Chicago group home for disabled children.

name: Lawrence Bittaker
victimProfile: Teenage girls aged 13 to 18, abducted while walking or hitchhiking in the South Bay and San Fernando Valley areas of Los Angeles County
captureMethod: A former fellow inmate to whom Roy Norris had described the killings went to police, and a surviving rape victim identified Bittaker from a photographic lineup, leading to both men's arrests on November 20, 1979.
sentence: Death (March 1981) for five counts of first-degree murder; affirmed by the California Supreme Court in 1989
fateDetail: Died of natural causes on death row at San Quentin State Prison on December 13, 2019, aged 79
summary: Died on death row in 2019. Lawrence Bittaker and accomplice Roy Norris, the 'Tool Box Killers', kidnapped and murdered five teenage girls in Los Angeles County in 1979. A jury convicted Bittaker in 1981 and he was sentenced to death.
narrative: Lawrence Sigmund Bittaker (1940-2019) was an American serial killer who, with accomplice Roy Lewis Norris, kidnapped and murdered five teenage girls in Los Angeles County, California, between June and October 1979. Because of the hand tools used on the victims, the pair became known as the "Tool Box Killers." A Los Angeles County jury convicted Bittaker in February 1981 of five counts of first-degree murder and 21 related felonies, and he was sentenced to death in March 1981. The California Supreme Court affirmed in 1989. He was never executed: the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation (CDCR) reported that he died of natural causes on death row at San Quentin State Prison on December 13, 2019, aged 79.

According to the California Supreme Court's opinion in People v. Bittaker (1989), Bittaker bought a van with sliding doors to make seizing victims easier. The victims, as named by CDCR and the court record, were Lucinda Lynn Schaefer, 16, abducted on June 24, 1979, in Redondo Beach; Andrea Joy Hall, 18, picked up while hitchhiking on Pacific Coast Highway on July 8; Jacqueline Doris Gilliam, 15, and Jacqueline Leah Lamp, 13, taken from a bus stop near Hermosa Beach on September 2; and Shirley Lynette Ledford, 16, abducted on October 31 while hitchhiking home in Sunland-Tujunga. The girls were driven into the San Gabriel Mountains, sexually assaulted and killed. Ledford's body was found on a Sunland lawn the next morning. The bodies of Schaefer and Hall were never recovered; the remains of Gilliam and Lamp were found in February 1980 after Norris agreed to help locate them.

The investigation began in November 1979 when, according to the Wikipedia article, Norris described the killings to a former fellow inmate, who consulted an attorney and then went to the police. The court opinion records that a woman who had survived an abduction and rape in September 1979 identified Bittaker from a photographic lineup, supporting the arrest warrant. Norris was arrested in Hermosa Beach on November 20, 1979, and Bittaker the same day at a Burbank motel. A tape recording of Ledford's abuse and photographs of victims, found in the van, were later used at trial.

Under a plea agreement described in the court opinion, Norris pleaded guilty to five counts of murder without special circumstances, two counts of rape and one count of robbery, agreed to help locate the bodies and to testify against Bittaker, and, prosecutors having agreed not to seek death, was sentenced to 45 years to life.

Bittaker's trial opened in Los Angeles County Superior Court in Torrance on January 19, 1981, before Judge Thomas Fredericks. United Press International reported the guilty verdicts on February 17, 1981; CDCR recorded convictions on all 26 counts, including kidnapping, conspiracy, rape, sodomy and firearm possession. The jury found 38 special circumstances true and returned a death verdict a week later. Bittaker testified that Norris had framed him and that he did not learn the girls had died until after his arrest. Judge Fredericks sentenced him to death on March 24, 1981 (CDCR lists March 22), and he was received on San Quentin's death row on March 30.

On June 22, 1989, a unanimous California Supreme Court, in an opinion by Justice Allen Broussard, affirmed the conviction and death sentence, holding that a restriction on death-penalty questioning of prospective jurors was erroneous but not prejudicial. According to the Wikipedia article, the United States Supreme Court declined to review the case in June 1990, execution dates set for 1989 and 1991 were stayed, and in 1993 a court declared Bittaker a vexatious litigant after he filed dozens of lawsuits. Norris died of natural causes on February 24, 2020, aged 72, at the California Medical Facility in Vacaville, the Associated Press reported.

Bittaker was born on September 27, 1940, in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. According to the Wikipedia article, he met Norris in 1977 at the California Men's Colony in San Luis Obispo, where Norris was serving a sentence for rape; Bittaker was paroled in October 1978 and Norris in January 1979. The court opinion notes that Bittaker was known in prison as "Pliers Bittaker" for the stories he told about torturing women.

summary: Died on death row in 2020. Lonnie Franklin Jr., the Grim Sleeper, was convicted by a Los Angeles jury in 2016 of 10 murders and one attempted murder in South Los Angeles between 1985 and 2007, and was caught in 2010 through familial DNA.
narrative: Lonnie David Franklin Jr., known as the Grim Sleeper, was convicted by a Los Angeles County jury on May 5, 2016, of 10 counts of first-degree murder and one count of attempted murder for attacks on women and girls in South Los Angeles between 1985 and 2007. According to the Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office, the jury found true the special circumstance of multiple murders, and Superior Court Judge Kathleen Kennedy sentenced him to death on August 10, 2016. He died on death row at San Quentin State Prison on March 28, 2020, at age 67. Prosecutors presented evidence of four uncharged killings at the penalty phase, and CBS Los Angeles reported that prosecutors said he may have had as many as 25 victims. Franklin never confessed.

The District Attorney's conviction announcement lists the 1980s victims by the date their bodies were found: Debra Jackson, 29, on August 10, 1985; Henrietta Wright, 34, on August 12, 1986; Barbara Ware, 23, on January 10, 1987; Bernita Sparks, 26, on April 16, 1987; Mary Lowe, 26, on November 1, 1987; Lachrica Jefferson, 22, on January 30, 1988; and Alicia Alexander, 18, on September 11, 1988. Eight of the ten victims were shot with the same .25-caliber firearm; two were strangled. On November 19, 1988, Enietra Washington, 30, was shot and pushed from Franklin's car; she survived and testified at trial as the attempted-murder victim.

The killings linked to the gun then stopped for roughly 13 years, the gap behind the nickname. The District Attorney identifies the later victims as Princess Berthomieux, 15, found strangled on March 9, 2002; Valerie McCorvey, 35, found on July 11, 2003; and Janecia Peters, 25, found shot inside a trash bag in a dumpster on January 1, 2007. According to Wikipedia, DNA from the Peters scene was connected to the earlier series in 2007, and the LAPD formed a task force.

The break came through familial DNA searching. An Associated Press report published by NBC News on July 7, 2010, said a DNA profile from Franklin's son, taken after a felony weapons conviction, closely resembled the crime-scene profiles. An undercover officer posing as a busboy collected items Franklin discarded at a pizza restaurant, and the DNA matched. Franklin, 57, was arrested at his home on 81st Street on July 7, 2010. The District Attorney's Office said the pistol used to kill Peters was recovered from his home under a search warrant.

The trial opened in February 2016. Deputy District Attorneys Beth Silverman and Marguerite Rizzo told jurors every victim was tied to the same killer through DNA, firearms evidence, or both; the defense argued an unidentified man was responsible. The jury deliberated about a day and a half before convicting Franklin on all counts. In the penalty phase, a woman testified that Franklin and two fellow soldiers had kidnapped and raped her in Germany in 1974. The jury recommended death on June 6, 2016. At sentencing, more than 15 family members addressed the court; CBS Los Angeles reported that Judge Kennedy denied a motion for a new trial.

The California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation (CDCR) said Franklin arrived on death row on August 17, 2016; CDCR reported that staff found him unresponsive in his cell at about 7:20 p.m. on March 28, 2020, and that he was pronounced dead at 7:43 p.m. with no signs of trauma; the department's register of condemned inmates who have died later recorded the cause as natural causes. NBC News reported that community members had long said police were slow to act because the victims were Black, poor and often drug users or sex workers.

Franklin was born in Los Angeles on August 30, 1952, according to Wikipedia, and served in the U.S. Army, where a West German court convicted him in 1974 over the kidnapping and rape of a teenage girl; he was dishonorably discharged in 1975. The AP reported that he worked as an LAPD garage attendant from 1981, became a city refuse collector in 1982, and left city employment in 1989. He lived for decades in the neighborhood where the bodies were found.

summary: Died in prison. Nannie Doss pleaded guilty in 1955 to poisoning her fifth husband, Samuel Doss, in Tulsa, Oklahoma, confessed to killing four husbands, and is linked to as many as 11 family deaths from 1927 to 1954. She died at the Oklahoma State Penitentiary in 1965.
narrative: Nannie Doss, born Nancy Agnes Hazel, was a serial poisoner whose victims were members of her own family in Alabama, North Carolina, Kansas and Oklahoma between 1927 and 1954. She was convicted of one murder: on May 17, 1955, she pleaded guilty in Tulsa, Oklahoma, to killing her fifth husband, Samuel Doss, and was sentenced to life imprisonment. According to the Encyclopedia of Alabama, she confessed under interrogation to killing four husbands. The Wikipedia article and an Oklahoma Gazette retrospective attribute as many as 11 deaths to her, among them two of her daughters, her mother, a sister, a mother-in-law and two grandchildren. She was never charged in any death other than that of Samuel Doss.

The Encyclopedia of Alabama records that she married Charles Braggs in 1921, at about 16, after the two met at the Linen Thread Company in Anniston, Alabama. Two of their four daughters died in 1927, with the deaths attributed at the time to food poisoning. The couple divorced in 1928, and Braggs was the only one of her five husbands to survive the marriage. In 1929 she married Frank Harrelson, whom she met through a lonely hearts column. Harrelson died on September 15, 1945; by her later account, she had put rat poison in his whiskey. A grandson, Robert, died of asphyxia at age two while in her care, and she collected a $500 life insurance policy.

Her third husband, Arlie Lanning of Lexington, North Carolina, died of what was recorded as heart failure, with no autopsy performed; the Encyclopedia of Alabama dates his death to 1950, while the Oklahoma Gazette gives 1952. The Wikipedia article states that Lanning's mother died in her sleep while Doss lived in the household, and that her sister Dovie died soon after Doss came to stay with her. In October 1952 she married Richard L. Morton of Emporia, Kansas. Her mother, Louisa Hazle, came to live with the couple and died within days, in January 1953. Morton died on May 19, 1953, after, the Encyclopedia of Alabama reports, drinking coffee laced with arsenic.

In June 1953 she married Samuel Doss, a Nazarene minister, in Tulsa, Oklahoma. In the autumn of 1954 he was hospitalised with a severe digestive illness, was sent home on October 5 and died about a week later, on October 12 according to the Wikipedia article. His physician insisted on an autopsy, which found a large quantity of arsenic. Doss was arrested in Tulsa in October 1954 and, during questioning, confessed to killing four husbands; the Encyclopedia of Alabama reports she did so in exchange for being allowed to keep a romance magazine. Her habit of laughing while recounting the deaths produced the nickname the Giggling Granny. The same source states that exhumations reportedly confirmed rat poison or arsenic in several of the bodies.

Oklahoma prosecuted her for a single count of murder, that of Samuel Doss. The prosecutor, according to the Wikipedia article, was J. Howard Edmondson, later governor of Oklahoma. She pleaded guilty on May 17, 1955, and received a life sentence; the Wikipedia article and a syndicated history column published by the Albuquerque Journal both report that the state did not seek the death penalty because she was a woman. The Encyclopedia of Alabama notes that North Carolina, Kansas and Alabama also brought charges, but she was never tried outside Oklahoma.

She served her sentence at the Oklahoma State Penitentiary in McAlester, where she died of leukemia in the prison hospital ward on June 2, 1965, at age 59. She was buried at Oak Hill Memorial Park in McAlester. The Oklahoma Gazette has written that her case figures in the history of Oklahoma's Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, as an example of suspicious deaths that went uninvestigated before the state had a medical examiner system.

She was born on November 4, 1905, in Blue Mountain, Calhoun County, Alabama, one of five children of Jim and Louisa Hazle. The Encyclopedia of Alabama describes her father as abusive and says he kept the children out of school to work the family farm. At about age seven she suffered a head injury in a train incident, which she later blamed for headaches and blackouts.
