summary: Died in prison 1996. Jacksonville drifter convicted of six Florida murders (1980-1983); two death sentences reduced to life. Confessed with Henry Lee Lucas to many more, then recanted. Named by police in 2008 as Adam Walsh's killer; never charged.
narrative: Ottis Elwood Toole was a Jacksonville, Florida drifter and arsonist convicted of six murders committed in Florida between 1980 and 1983. A jury convicted him in 1984 of the arson death of George Sonnenberg and he was sentenced to death; the Florida Supreme Court affirmed the conviction but vacated the sentence in 1985, and he was resentenced to life. A second 1984 death sentence, for strangling a 19-year-old Tallahassee woman, was also reduced to life, and in 1991 he pleaded guilty to four more Jacksonville murders. With Henry Lee Lucas he confessed to many more killings, most never corroborated and later recanted. He died in Florida State Prison in September 1996.

According to the Florida Supreme Court's opinion in Toole v. State (No. 65,378, November 25, 1985), a Jacksonville boarding house burned on January 4, 1982, and resident George Sonnenberg died of his injuries. Toole, a handyman for the owner, was questioned while incarcerated at Lake Butler on an unrelated offense and confessed to setting the fire after arguing with Sonnenberg; at trial he denied it and said he signed the statement to get back to Jacksonville. UPI reported that Sonnenberg, 64, died a week after the fire and that Toole was already serving 20 years for burning two abandoned Jacksonville houses in 1983.

The jury found Toole guilty of first-degree felony murder on April 28, 1984, and recommended death; Circuit Judge James L. Harrison imposed the sentence in May 1984, UPI reported. The Florida Supreme Court affirmed the conviction but held that the trial judge had wrongly refused a jury instruction on extreme mental or emotional disturbance, given defense evidence of pyromania, borderline intellectual functioning and a personality disorder, and ordered a new sentencing hearing. According to Fox News and the Wikipedia article, this and a second 1984 death sentence, for the February 1983 strangulation of a 19-year-old Tallahassee woman, were both reduced to life imprisonment.

Toole's notoriety rests mainly on his association with Henry Lee Lucas, whom he met in Jacksonville in the 1970s. After Lucas was arrested in Texas in June 1983 and began confessing to hundreds of murders, Toole first denied involvement and then backed many of Lucas's claims. UPI reported in 1984 that authorities said the pair had admitted to more than 300 killings, though investigators doubted many of them; Wikipedia records Toole's own uncorroborated claim of 108 murders with Lucas. Reviewers later concluded that Lucas could not have travelled the distances his confessions required, and both men recanted. The courts convicted Toole of six murders; the confessions remain unverified.

In October 1983, while in prison, Toole confessed to the July 27, 1981 abduction and killing of six-year-old Adam Walsh from a Sears store at a Hollywood, Florida mall. NBC News reported that fishermen found the child's severed head in a canal near Vero Beach two weeks later and that his body was never found. Toole confessed and recanted repeatedly; ABC News counted 24 documented confessions. Authorities lost the bloodstained carpet from Toole's car and then the car itself, preventing DNA testing. He was never charged in the case.

On December 16, 2008, twelve years after Toole's death, Hollywood Police Chief Chadwick Wagner announced that the department considered Toole responsible for Adam Walsh's murder and closed the case, acknowledging missteps and apologizing to the Walsh family, NBC News reported. No new physical or DNA evidence was presented. It is a police conclusion, not a court verdict. Adam's father, John Walsh, has said he believes Toole was the killer.

In 1991 Toole pleaded guilty in Jacksonville to four further murders and received four life sentences, according to Fox News and the Wikipedia article. He died on September 15, 1996, aged 49, at Florida State Prison in Raiford of liver failure; NBC News reported that no relative claimed his body and he was buried on prison grounds. Toole was born in Jacksonville on March 5, 1947. The Wikipedia article reports a childhood of abuse, early arrests and repeated fire-setting.

summary: On death row in California since 1989. Randy Kraft was convicted by an Orange County jury of murdering 16 young men between 1972 and 1983; a coded list found at his 1983 arrest is believed to reference up to 67 victims in California, Oregon and Michigan.
narrative: Randy Steven Kraft is a California serial killer convicted of murdering 16 young men in Southern California between 1972 and 1983. According to the California Supreme Court's 2000 opinion in People v. Kraft, an Orange County jury convicted him in May 1989 of 16 counts of first-degree murder, one count of sodomy and one count of mayhem, and he was sentenced to death on November 29, 1989. Investigators attribute more deaths to him: the Orange County Sheriff's Department said in 2025 that it believes he is responsible for more than 60 killings in California, six in Oregon and two in Michigan. He has never confessed and, the Associated Press reported in 2025, denies killing anyone.

The court opinion sets out the 16 murders. The earliest victim, Marine Edward Daniel Moore, was found strangled near a Long Beach-area freeway off-ramp on December 26, 1972. Others followed through the 1970s, including Ronald Wiebe, Keith Crotwell, Mark Hall, Scott Hughes, Roland Young, Richard Keith, Keith Klingbeil, Michael Inderbieten, Donald Crisel and Robert Loggins, with a final cluster in 1983 of Eric Church, Geoffrey Nelson and Rodger DeVaul. Most were strangled with a ligature or suffocated after being given alcohol and sedatives, and their bodies were left beside freeways in Orange and Los Angeles counties. The opinion notes that physical evidence, including a thumbprint at the Hall scene and victims' property and photographs found in his home and car, linked Kraft to eight murders; the rest rested on the common method and his written list.

Kraft was arrested early on May 14, 1983. According to the opinion, California Highway Patrol officers saw his car weaving on Interstate 5 in southern Orange County and arrested him for drunk driving; his passenger, 25-year-old Marine Terry Gambrel, was dead of ligature strangulation, with a vial of Kraft's prescription sedative on the floor. A notebook in the car held a sheet of 61 cryptic handwritten entries. Prosecutors linked 13 to the charged murders, eight to Oregon and Michigan killings and 21 to uncharged victims, hence the press name Scorecard Killer.

The trial opened in Orange County Superior Court in September 1988 and ran about 13 months, according to reporting summarized in the Wikipedia article. The jury returned guilty verdicts on May 12, 1989 and a death verdict on August 11, 1989. Death was imposed on the 11 murders committed after 1978; the five earlier murders drew consecutive 25-years-to-life terms, stayed. The CDCR condemned list records the sentence date as November 29, 1989.

In the penalty phase, the opinion records, prosecutors presented eight uncharged murders in Oregon and Michigan. Oregon victims found near Interstate 5 between July 1980 and December 1982 included Michael O'Fallon, Michael Cluck, Brian Whitcher, Anthony Silveira and an unidentified man; travel records placed Kraft in the Portland area on each date, and several victims' belongings were in his home. In Michigan, Dennis Alt and Christopher Schoenborn were found strangled in Kent County on December 9, 1982, last seen at the Grand Rapids hotel where Kraft was staying.

On August 10, 2000, the California Supreme Court unanimously affirmed the judgment in its entirety in an opinion by Justice Werdegar. Kraft remains under sentence of death; California executions have been halted by a gubernatorial moratorium since 2019, and official and AP reporting in 2023 and 2025 placed him at San Quentin.

DNA work has continued to develop the case. In November 2023 the Orange County Sheriff's Department used genetic genealogy to identify a John Doe found in Laguna Hills in 1974 as Michael Ray Schlicht, 17, of Cedar Rapids, Iowa, calling him a presumed early Kraft victim. In May 2025 the department and Oregon State Police identified the 1980 Oregon John Doe as Larry Eugene Parks, a 30-year-old Vietnam veteran, and Oregon State Police named Kraft the sole person of interest.

Kraft was born in Long Beach, California, on March 19, 1945, according to the Wikipedia article, graduated from Claremont Men's College in 1968 and received a general discharge from the U.S. Air Force in 1969. He worked as a computer programmer; the court opinion notes his employment with Lear Siegler from 1980 to 1983, whose business travel coincided with the Oregon and Michigan murders.

summary: Imprisoned since 1980. Richard Cottingham, the "Torso Killer", was convicted at trials in New Jersey and New York (1981, 1982, 1984) of five murders, later pleaded guilty to four more, and has confessed to 11 others closed without charges.
narrative: Richard Francis Cottingham, known as the "Torso Killer" and the "Times Square Killer", murdered women and girls in New Jersey and New York between 1967 and 1980. Courts have convicted him of nine murders: five by trial verdicts in Bergen County, New Jersey (1981 and 1982) and Manhattan (1984), and four by guilty pleas in 2010, 2021 and 2022. Prosecutors have also accepted his confessions to 11 further killings closed without charges. NBC News reported that he has claimed up to 100 murders, a figure authorities have not confirmed.

The crimes he was tried for surfaced in 1979 and 1980. On December 2, 1979, Deedeh Goodarzi, 22, and an unidentified woman were found decapitated in a burning room at the Travel Inn Motor Hotel in Manhattan, the source of the "Torso Killer" name. In May 1980 Valerie Ann Street, 19, was found strangled under a bed at the Quality Inn in Hasbrouck Heights, New Jersey, and Mary Ann Jean Reyner, 25, was found stabbed and burned at the Seville Hotel in Manhattan. The December 1977 strangling of Maryann Carr, 26, in Little Ferry was later tied to him as well.

On May 22, 1980, Cottingham brought Leslie Ann O'Dell, 18, to the same Hasbrouck Heights motel. According to the Wikipedia account, she escaped into the hallway and screamed, staff called police, and he was arrested as he tried to leave. Two women who survived 1978 attacks, Karen Schilt and Susan Geiger, identified him in a lineup, and he was indicted in Bergen County and charged in New York with the three Manhattan killings.

A Radford University case summary citing New York Times coverage records the three trials. In June 1981 he was convicted in Bergen County of murdering Street and of kidnapping and assaulting Schilt, Geiger and O'Dell, and on July 25, 1981 was sentenced to 173 to 197 years. On October 12, 1982, he was convicted of the Carr murder in what the summary describes as a non-jury trial and sentenced to 25 years to life. On July 9, 1984, a Manhattan jury convicted him of murdering Goodarzi, the unidentified woman and Reyner; he was sentenced to 75 years to life.

Interviews by Bergen County Chief of Detectives Robert Anzilotti produced later admissions. In 2010 Cottingham pleaded guilty to the 1967 strangling of Nancy Schiava Vogel, 29, found in her car in Ridgefield Park, and received a life sentence, according to New Jersey 101.5 and Oxygen. In January 2020 the prosecutor's office announced he had admitted strangling Jacalyn Harp, 13, Irene Blase, 18, and Denise Falasca, 15, in 1968 and 1969; those cases were cleared without charges. On April 27, 2021, he pleaded guilty before Judge Keith Bachmann to murdering Mary Ann Pryor, 17, and Lorraine Marie Kelly, 16, who vanished hitchhiking on August 9, 1974 and were found in Montvale five days later. The prosecutor's office said he admitted drowning them in a motel bathtub; NBC News reported the plea agreement called for two concurrent life sentences.

After a DNA match, Nassau County, New York indicted him in 2022 for the 1968 killing of Diane Cusick, 23, found in her car outside the Green Acres Mall in Valley Stream. On December 5, 2022, he pleaded guilty before Judge Caryn Fink and was sentenced to 25 years to life, and the Long Island Press reported he admitted killing four other Nassau women in 1972 and 1973, Mary Beth Heinz, Laverne Moye, Sheila Heiman and Maria Emerita Rosado Nieves, under a non-prosecution agreement. According to the Wikipedia article, Rockland County accepted confessions to two more killings in 2022 and Bergen County added the 1967 killing of Mary Ann Della Sala in 2023. In January 2026, NBC New York reported that Fair Lawn police had closed the 1965 killing of Alys Eberhardt, 18, on his confession; he was not charged.

Cottingham was born on November 25, 1946 in the Bronx and raised in Bergen County. He worked as a computer operator in Manhattan, married in 1970 and had three children, and lived in Lodi, New Jersey when arrested. He is now held at South Woods State Prison in Bridgeton, according to the Wikipedia article and 2022 court reporting.

victims.suspected: 15 or more (13 convictions plus two San Francisco killings attributed by police)

victimProfile: Residents attacked in their homes at night, from a 9-year-old girl to adults in their 60s to 80s; women were often sexually assaulted and men shot
captureMethod: A fingerprint lifted from the rear-view mirror of an abandoned stolen car was matched to his 1984 arrest record, his photograph was released, and residents of East Los Angeles recognized and held him after an attempted carjacking.

summary: Died on death row in 2013. Richard Ramirez, the Night Stalker, was convicted by a Los Angeles jury in 1989 of 13 murders, 5 attempted murders, 11 sexual assaults and 14 burglaries committed in 1984 and 1985, and sentenced to death.
narrative: Richard Ramirez, known as the Night Stalker, carried out a series of night-time home invasions in the Los Angeles area between June 1984 and August 1985, with related attacks in San Francisco and Orange County. On September 20, 1989, a Los Angeles County jury convicted him of 12 counts of first-degree murder, one count of second-degree murder, five counts of attempted murder, 11 sexual assault counts and 14 counts of first-degree burglary, according to the California Supreme Court's 2006 opinion in People v. Ramirez. He was sentenced to death on November 7, 1989, and died of natural causes on June 7, 2013, while on death row at San Quentin.

The first killing in the Los Angeles case was that of Jennie Vincow, 79, found dead in her Glassell Park apartment on June 28, 1984; a fingerprint was recovered from a window screen, the court opinion says. The attacks resumed on March 17, 1985, when Dayle Okazaki was shot dead in Rosemead and her roommate Maria Hernandez survived; within the hour Tsai-Lian Yu was shot dead in Monterey Park. Over the following months Vincent and Maxine Zazzara were killed in Whittier, William Doi in Monterey Park, Mabel Bell in Monrovia, Mary Cannon in Arcadia, Joyce Nelson in Monterey Park, Maxon and Lela Kneiding in Glendale, Chainarong Khovananth in Sun Valley and Elyas Abowath in Diamond Bar on August 8, 1985. Several surviving women were raped, and pentagrams were drawn at some scenes.

Investigators tied the crimes together through ballistics from a .22-caliber pistol, prints from Avia athletic shoes and eyewitness descriptions, according to the opinion. On August 18, 1985, Peter Pan was shot dead in San Francisco and his wife Barbara survived, an attack San Francisco authorities linked to the series. After an August 24 attack in Mission Viejo in which Bill Carns was shot and survived, a witness noted the suspect's car. The stolen Toyota was found abandoned in Los Angeles on August 28, and a fingerprint from its rear-view mirror was matched to Ramirez's record from a 1984 auto-theft arrest, according to Wikipedia's account. Police released his photograph.

On August 31, 1985, Ramirez tried to steal cars in East Los Angeles; residents who recognized him from news reports chased, struck and held him until police arrived, the court opinion records. At the station he made spontaneous statements admitting the killings.

Ramirez was charged with 43 offenses in Los Angeles County; the Los Angeles Times reported in November 1987 that one murder count was dismissed, leaving 13. Jury selection began on July 22, 1988. The jury returned guilty verdicts on all counts on September 20, 1989, found special circumstances of multiple murder, burglary, rape, sodomy and oral copulation true, and returned a death verdict. The judge imposed the death sentence on November 7, 1989.

On August 7, 2006, the California Supreme Court affirmed the convictions and death sentence, rejecting challenges to venue, severance, counsel substitution, competency and the admission of crime-scene photographs. He never went to trial on the San Francisco charges arising from the Pan shooting. In October 2009, San Francisco police said DNA matched Ramirez to the April 10, 1984, killing of nine-year-old Mei Leung in an apartment building basement; CBS News reported the match, and no charges followed. Ramirez married Doreen Lioy at San Quentin on October 3, 1996.

Ramirez died at Marin General Hospital in Greenbrae on June 7, 2013, at age 53. The California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation lists the death as natural causes, and the Marin County coroner later attributed it to complications of B-cell lymphoma, according to reporting cited by Wikipedia. He had been on death row for more than 23 years.

Ramirez was born Ricardo Leyva Muñoz Ramírez in El Paso, Texas, on February 29, 1960, the youngest of five children of Mexican immigrant parents. Accounts cited by Wikipedia describe childhood head injuries, epilepsy and early drug use. He dropped out of high school, moved to California in 1982 and funded a cocaine habit through burglaries before the murders began.

summary: Died in prison. Robert Berdella pleaded guilty in 1988 to murdering six young men held captive at his Kansas City, Missouri home between 1984 and 1987. Sentenced to life without parole, he died at the Missouri State Penitentiary in October 1992.
narrative: Robert Berdella is an American serial killer who pleaded guilty in 1988 to murdering six young men in Kansas City, Missouri, between 1984 and 1987. He was never tried: on his pleas he was convicted of two counts of first-degree murder and four counts of second-degree murder, received six life sentences, and died in the Missouri State Penitentiary in October 1992. Prosecutors agreed not to seek the death penalty in exchange for his confessions, according to United Press International reporting at the time.

According to the Wikipedia article, the first victim was Jerry Howell, 19, who died on July 5, 1984, after being held at Berdella's house in the Hyde Park neighborhood. Five more men died there over the next three years: Robert Sheldon, 20, in April 1985; Mark Wallace, 27, in June 1985; Walter Ferris, 25, in September 1985; Todd Stoops, 23, in July 1986; and Larry Pearson, 20, in 1987. Each man was held captive at the house before he died, in most cases of asphyxiation, and the bodies were never recovered. UPI reported in May 1988 that the families of Howell and Ferris had long said the men were last seen with Berdella.

The case broke on April 2, 1988, when a 22-year-old man, later identified as Christopher Bryson, escaped from the house by jumping from a second-floor window and reached police wearing only a dog collar. Berdella was arrested the same day and charged with seven counts of forcible sodomy, one count of first-degree assault and one count of felonious restraint. Police began digging up the yard on April 3 and seized more than 200 photographs of men being abused. A skull found inside the house was identified on May 10, 1988, through hospital X-rays and dental records as Robert Sheldon, and two days later a second skull dug from the back yard was identified by dental records as Larry Pearson, UPI reported.

A grand jury indicted Berdella for Pearson's murder on July 22, 1988. In early August he pleaded guilty to first-degree murder in Pearson's death before Judge Alvin C. Randall and was sentenced to life in prison without parole; later that month he pleaded guilty to forcible sodomy and felonious restraint in the Bryson case, receiving a further life term and seven years, with the remaining counts dropped. In September he pleaded not guilty to five additional murder charges. UPI reported on December 19, 1988, that after a week of meetings with prosecutors, public defenders and detectives at the county jail, Berdella had agreed to confess to the five remaining killings in exchange for prosecutors not recommending death. That day, according to the Wikipedia article, he pleaded guilty before Jackson County Circuit Judge Robert Meyers to first-degree murder in the death of Sheldon and second-degree murder in the deaths of Howell, Wallace, Ferris and Stoops, and received five further concurrent life sentences.

Berdella was sent to the Missouri State Penitentiary in Jefferson City, with a brief period at Potosi Correctional Center for his own protection. He died on October 8, 1992, aged 43, after complaining of chest pains; he was pronounced dead at a hospital in Columbia, Missouri, and the cause was recorded as a heart attack. The Pitch, a Kansas City weekly, reported in 2004 that a minister said Berdella had telephoned him shortly before his death claiming prison officials were withholding his heart medication. His house on Charlotte Street was sold and demolished, and the lot was later deeded to the Hyde Park Neighborhood Association.

Berdella was born on January 31, 1949, in Cuyahoga Falls, Ohio. By the 1980s he ran a stall at the Westport Flea Market in Kansas City, known as Bob's Bazaar Bizarre and lived alone at 4315 Charlotte Street. He was described in court proceedings as having a depressive personality disorder and sexual sadism disorder, according to the Wikipedia article. His case was the subject of Tom Jackman and Troy Cole's book Rites of Burial (1992) and Ben Meade's 2004 documentary Bazaar Bizarre.

summary: Convicted; died on California's death row in 2021. Rodney Alcala, the Dating Game Killer, was convicted in 2010 of five murders in Southern California (1977-1979) after two overturned Samsoe convictions, and pleaded guilty in 2012 to two 1970s Manhattan murders.
narrative: Rodney James Alcala, known as the Dating Game Killer, was convicted of seven murders committed in California and New York between 1971 and 1979. In February 2010 an Orange County jury found him guilty of five counts of first-degree murder and he was sentenced to death; in December 2012 he pleaded guilty in Manhattan to two further murders and received 25 years to life. He had twice before been convicted and sentenced to death for one of the California killings, the 1979 murder of 12-year-old Robin Samsoe, but both judgments were overturned on appeal. He died of natural causes on California's death row on 24 July 2021.

According to NBC New York's report on the 2013 sentencing, the earliest murder was that of Cornelia Crilley, a 23-year-old flight attendant strangled with a stocking in her Manhattan apartment in June 1971. Ellen Jane Hover, 23, disappeared from Manhattan in July 1977; her remains were found the next year in Westchester County, and her calendar noted a lunch with a photographer using one of Alcala's aliases. In California, the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation (CDCR) lists the five 2010 convictions as the murders of Jill Barcomb, 18, and Georgia Wixted, 27, in 1977; Charlotte Lamb, 32, in 1978; and Jill Parenteau, 21, and Robin Samsoe, 12, in 1979.

The Ninth Circuit's 2003 opinion in Alcala v. Woodford describes the Samsoe case. She left a friend's apartment just after 3 p.m. on 20 June 1979 and never arrived; her body was found in a remote ravine about fifty miles away almost two weeks later, too decomposed to establish a cause of death. Alcala was arrested on 24 July 1979. The circumstantial case rested on beachgoers approached by a photographer, a witness who placed him near the body, and earrings identified as Samsoe's, found in a Seattle storage locker he rented after the disappearance. The locker also held a large collection of photographs of women and girls that police later released publicly to identify possible victims.

Alcala was convicted and sentenced to death in 1980. In 1984 the California Supreme Court reversed because the trial court had erroneously admitted evidence of his prior offences, and ordered a new trial. A second jury convicted him in 1986 and he was again sentenced to death; the state supreme court affirmed in 1992. In 2001 a federal district judge conditionally granted his habeas petition, and in June 2003 the Ninth Circuit affirmed, finding ineffective assistance of counsel on his alibi, the wrongful exclusion of a defence expert, and cumulative error that denied him a fair trial.

Before a third trial, DNA evidence connected Alcala to four unsolved Los Angeles County murders. In Alcala v. Superior Court (2008) the California Supreme Court held that those charges could be joined with the Orange County retrial. Alcala represented himself. On 25 February 2010 the jury found him guilty on all five counts, and he was sentenced to death in March 2010. ABC News reported that his closing argument cited his 1978 appearance as a contestant on The Dating Game, the source of his nickname.

Manhattan prosecutors indicted him in January 2011 for the Crilley and Hover murders after a cold-case review. He was extradited in 2012, pleaded guilty in December, and on 7 January 2013 was sentenced to a concurrent 25 years to life. In 2016 Wyoming prosecutors charged him with the murder of Christine Ruth Thornton, 28, whose 1982 remains were identified by relatives' DNA in 2015 after a sister recognised her in a storage-locker photograph, CBS News and CDCR reported; he was never extradited. Investigators have also linked him to other deaths in California, Washington, New York, New Hampshire and Arizona without further convictions.

Alcala was born Rodrigo Jacques Alcala Buquor in San Antonio, Texas, on 23 August 1943, and grew up near Los Angeles. He served in the Army before a medical discharge and later studied fine arts at UCLA. In 1968 he attacked an eight-year-old girl in Hollywood and fled; arrested in New Hampshire in 1971 under an alias, he was convicted in California and paroled in 1974, then paroled again in 1977 after a second assault conviction.

name: Shawn Grate
victimProfile: Women aged 23 to 43 in north-central Ohio, several of them vulnerable or living on the margins, including a door-to-door magazine seller
captureMethod: A woman he was holding captive in a vacant Ashland house called 911 on his phone while he slept, and police arrested him there and found two bodies
sentence: Death (Ashland County, June 2018), affirmed by the Ohio Supreme Court in 2020; life without parole plus consecutive terms in Richland County (2019) and Marion County (2019)
fateDetail: Ohio death row; held at Chillicothe Correctional Institution according to the state's 2021 U.S. Supreme Court brief
summary: On Ohio's death row. Shawn Grate was convicted of killing five women in Ashland, Richland and Marion counties between 2006 and 2016; a captive's 911 call from his Ashland house led to his arrest in September 2016.
narrative: Shawn Grate is an Ohio man convicted of murdering five women in Ashland, Richland and Marion counties between 2006 and 2016. An Ashland County jury convicted him in May 2018 of the aggravated murders of Stacey Stanley and Elizabeth Griffith, and he was sentenced to death; he later pleaded guilty to three more killings in Richland and Marion counties and received life without parole in each. According to the Ohio Attorney General's 2021 brief to the U.S. Supreme Court, he fully confessed to the two Ashland murders and the kidnapping of a third woman, and the Richland Source reported that authorities said he admitted to killing five women in all. The Ohio Supreme Court upheld the death sentence in December 2020.

Prosecutors consider his first victim Dana Nicole Lowrey, 23, of Louisiana. The Associated Press reported that she was selling magazines door-to-door in Ohio when Grate stabbed her at his home in 2006; her remains were found on Victory Road in Marion in 2007 but went unidentified for more than a decade. Grate confessed in 2016 to killing a woman whose name he did not know, and in June 2019 investigators identified her through a DNA match with one of her daughters, with help from the DNA Doe Project. In Richland County, Rebekah Leicy's body was found in March 2015, about a month after she went missing; her death was initially ruled an overdose, and News 5 Cleveland reported the case was reopened after Grate's Ashland confessions. Candace Cunningham's body was found behind a burned-down house in Madison Township in September 2016.

The Ashland crimes ended on September 13, 2016. According to the state's brief and news reports, a woman Grate had held for days in a vacant house on Covert Court partly freed herself and, while he slept, whispered a 911 call on his phone saying she had been abducted. Ashland police arrested Grate and found in the house the bodies of Stanley, 43, and Griffith, 29, both reported missing. Autopsies found both had been strangled, and prosecutors said Grate confessed to detectives. The survivor has not been publicly named in the sources used here.

An Ashland County grand jury indicted Grate in September 2016 on 23 felony counts, including aggravated murder, kidnapping and rape. His lawyers entered a not guilty by reason of insanity plea but withdrew it in April 2017 after two experts found he was not insane. On May 2, 2018, Grate pleaded guilty to 15 counts, leaving the remaining eight, including the aggravated murders, to a jury. After a trial before Judge Ronald Forsthoefel at which prosecutors played his recorded statements, the jury convicted him on all eight counts on May 7, 2018, after deliberating a little over three hours, CBS News and the AP reported. The jury recommended death, and on June 1, 2018, the court sentenced him to death, according to Wikipedia; an initial September 13, 2018 execution date was stayed by his appeal.

On March 1, 2019, Grate pleaded guilty in Richland County to aggravated murder in Leicy's death and murder in Cunningham's death, plus two counts of gross abuse of a corpse; News 5 Cleveland reported a sentence of life without parole, 15 years to life and two 12-month terms, all consecutive. On September 11, 2019, he pleaded guilty in Marion County to Lowrey's aggravated murder and related counts and was sentenced to life without parole plus 16 years, consecutive to his other sentences; the AP reported that he apologized before sentencing.

On December 10, 2020, the Ohio Supreme Court unanimously affirmed the Ashland County convictions and death sentence in State v. Grate, 2020-Ohio-5584, rejecting claims of trial error and ineffective counsel. Grate petitioned the U.S. Supreme Court in 2021; the state's response noted he then had no scheduled execution date. Wikipedia reports that a March 19, 2025 execution date was later set and delayed amid continuing appeals.

Grate was born in Marion, Ohio, on August 8, 1976. According to Wikipedia, his parents divorced in 1982, he graduated from River Valley High School in 1995 and he had a felony burglary case in 1997. At the time of his arrest he was squatting in the vacant Covert Court house in Ashland.

summary: Released in 2022 after serving about 19 years. Pleaded guilty (Alford pleas) in 2004 to second-degree murder of Kathy Loreno and first-degree manslaughter of Ron Woodworth, boarders who died in her Pacific County, Washington home; her husband was convicted of killing her nephew.
narrative: Shelly Knotek, legally Michelle Knotek, is a Washington woman convicted in the deaths of two adults who lived in her rural home near Raymond, in Pacific County. On June 18, 2004, she entered Alford pleas in Pacific County Superior Court to second-degree murder in the death of Kathy Loreno, 36, and first-degree manslaughter in the death of Ronald Woodworth, 57, according to the Washington Court of Appeals opinion in State v. Knotek and Associated Press reporting. An Alford plea is a guilty plea in which the defendant maintains innocence while acknowledging a jury would likely convict. She was sentenced to 266 months, about 22 years, and released on November 8, 2022. A third death in the household, that of her nephew Shane Watson, was the subject of her husband David Knotek's separate guilty plea to second-degree murder; she was not convicted of it.

According to the Court of Appeals, in 1991 Knotek invited Loreno, a hairdresser she met at a South Bend salon, to live with her family. The opinion states that Knotek and her husband abused Loreno physically and mentally, causing severe weight loss and hypothermia, and that she died of the prolonged abuse. The Seattle Times reported that charging documents placed her death between April 1990 and December 1993; her mother reported her missing in 1994, and the Knoteks said she had run off with a truck driver. Per the opinion, David Knotek and Shane Watson burned and buried the body, and Knotek sent Loreno's family letters made to look as if they came from her.

Watson, Knotek's nephew, had lived with the family since his teens and vanished around the time of Loreno's disappearance. The Seattle Times reported that prosecutors alleged he was shot in a shed on the property between January 1993 and December 1994, and that the Knoteks had claimed he went to Alaska to fish. The Associated Press reported that David Knotek admitted shooting him.

In October 2001, according to the Court of Appeals, Knotek invited Woodworth, a Vietnam veteran who had helped her care for elderly clients, into the home, and the couple abused him in similar ways. The Seattle Times reported that prosecutors alleged the abuse included scalding his feet and that he died on about July 24, 2003. David Knotek buried the body in the backyard.

The case broke in August 2003 when Knotek's two older daughters contacted police about the treatment of Woodworth, per the Court of Appeals. The daughters, identified in Gregg Olsen's 2019 book If You Tell as Sami and Tori Knotek with their older sister, have since spoken publicly. Officers arrested the couple at their Monohon Landing Road home on August 8, 2003, and unearthed Woodworth's body. On August 13, prosecutors charged Michelle Knotek with two counts of first-degree murder and David Knotek with the first-degree murder of Watson, rendering criminal assistance and unlawful disposal of human remains. The Seattle Times also reported that South Bend police reopened an inquiry into the February 2002 death of James McClintock, 81, a client in Knotek's care; no charge resulted.

After the charges were reduced and the June 2004 Alford pleas entered, Judge Mark McCauley sentenced Knotek on August 19, 2004, to 164 months on the murder count and 102 months on the manslaughter count, consecutive, the top of the standard range and more than the roughly 17 years in the plea agreement. The Court of Appeals noted the judge said he would have gone higher but for Blakely v. Washington, decided six days after the plea. David Knotek was sentenced the following week to 179 months, the Chinook Observer reported. The Court of Appeals affirmed the denial of Knotek's motion to withdraw her plea on December 26, 2006.

The Chinook Observer reported that Knotek, then 68, was paroled from the Washington Corrections Center for Women on November 8, 2022, after just over 19 years, and was not expected to return to Pacific County. Wikipedia states David Knotek was released in 2016. The case was the subject of Olsen's book and of television programs.
Knotek was born Michelle Watson on April 15, 1954, according to Wikipedia.

name: Ted Bundy

captureMethod: Stopped by Pensacola police officer David Lee while driving a stolen car near the Alabama state line on February 15, 1978, six weeks after his second escape from Colorado custody.
sentence: Death, three times: two death sentences in July 1979 for the Chi Omega murders and one in February 1980 for the murder of Kimberly Leach; earlier, one to fifteen years in Utah for aggravated kidnapping (1976)
fateDetail: Electric chair, Florida State Prison, Bradford County, Florida; pronounced dead at 7:16 a.m. on January 24, 1989
summary: Executed in Florida in 1989. Ted Bundy was convicted of three murders in Florida and confessed to 30 killings of young women across Washington, Oregon, Utah, Colorado, Idaho and Florida between 1974 and 1978.
narrative: Ted Bundy, born Theodore Robert Cowell, was an American serial killer who murdered young women and girls in Washington, Oregon, Utah, Colorado, Idaho and Florida between 1974 and 1978. Florida juries convicted him of three murders: two Chi Omega sorority members at Florida State University in Tallahassee (1979) and 12-year-old Kimberly Leach of Lake City (1980), with a death sentence in each case. Before his execution he confessed to 30 homicides in seven states, according to Washington investigator Robert Keppel as quoted by The Associated Press; police had attributed about 20 killings to him before those confessions. Florida executed him on January 24, 1989.

The known crimes began in Seattle. According to the chronology in his Wikipedia article, Lynda Ann Healy, abducted on February 1, 1974, is counted as his first confirmed murder victim. Through 1974 five more young women vanished in Washington, including Georgann Hawkins (June 11) and, on the same July 14 afternoon, Janice Ott and Denise Naslund; Roberta Parks disappeared in Oregon on May 6. In recorded interviews released by the Washington attorney general's office and reported by the Deseret News, Bundy told Keppel how he lured, struck, handcuffed and strangled Hawkins and left her body outside Issaquah. He typically lured women by feigning injury or posing as an authority figure, then bludgeoned them and drove them to a remote site.

After Bundy moved to Utah in the autumn of 1974, Nancy Wilcox, Melissa Smith, Laura Aime and Debra Kent were killed there between October 1 and November 8. On the evening of November 8, at Fashion Place Mall in Murray, a man posing as a police officer lured Carol DaRonch into his car; she fought free. In 1975 Caryn Campbell vanished from Snowmass Village, Colorado, on January 12, followed by further disappearances in Colorado, Idaho and Utah through June 1975.

Utah Highway Patrol officer Bob Hayward arrested Bundy after a traffic stop in Granger, Utah, on August 16, 1975. DaRonch identified him in a lineup on October 2, 1975, and in 1976 a judge found him guilty of aggravated kidnapping after a bench trial; he was sentenced in June 1976 to one to fifteen years. Colorado then charged him with the Campbell murder. On June 7, 1977, he escaped from the Pitkin County Courthouse in Aspen, recaptured six days later. On December 30, 1977, he escaped again from the Garfield County jail in Glenwood Springs and made his way to Tallahassee.

In the early hours of January 15, 1978, an intruder attacked four women at the Chi Omega house, killing Margaret Bowman, 21, and Lisa Levy, 20, and injuring Kathy Kleiner and Karen Chandler; Cheryl Thomas was attacked nearby the same night and survived. On February 9, 1978, Kimberly Leach, 12, was taken from Lake City Junior High School; her remains were found near Suwannee River State Park on April 7. Pensacola officer David Lee arrested him in a stolen car on February 15, 1978.

The Chi Omega trial was moved to Miami before Judge Edward Cowart. Bite-mark testimony linked him to Levy. On July 24, 1979, the jury convicted him of two counts of first-degree murder, three counts of attempted first-degree murder and burglary, and Cowart imposed two death sentences. The Leach case was moved from Suwannee County to Orange County, where, as the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit later recounted, jury selection took place in January 1980; Bundy was convicted of first-degree murder and kidnapping and sentenced to death in February 1980.

The Florida Supreme Court affirmed both convictions (Bundy v. State, 1984 and 1985). The U.S. Supreme Court denied review of the Leach conviction on October 14, 1986, over dissents by Justices Brennan and Marshall. On July 7, 1988, the Eleventh Circuit in Bundy v. Dugger rejected his federal habeas petition finding that he had been competent to stand trial. In January 1989 Bundy admitted 30 homicides to Keppel and other investigators. He was executed in the electric chair at Florida State Prison on January 24, 1989.
Bundy was born on November 24, 1946, in Burlington, Vermont, and grew up in Tacoma, Washington. He remains an unconfirmed suspect in the 1961 disappearance of eight-year-old Ann Marie Burr in Tacoma.

summary: Imprisoned for life. Todd Kohlhepp, a South Carolina real estate agent, pleaded guilty in May 2017 to seven murders: the 2003 Superbike Motorsports shootings in Chesnee and three people killed on his Woodruff property in 2015 and 2016.
narrative: Todd Kohlhepp is a South Carolina real estate agent who pleaded guilty on May 26, 2017, to seven counts of murder committed in Spartanburg County between 2003 and 2016: the four Superbike Motorsports killings in Chesnee in November 2003 and three people killed on his rural property near Woodruff in 2015 and 2016. He received seven consecutive life sentences without parole under a plea agreement that took the death penalty off the table. No court has attributed further deaths to him, although he has since claimed, without specifics, that there are more victims.

The Superbike Motorsports killings were a cold case for 13 years. According to ABC News, shop owner Scott Ponder, 30, service manager Brian Lucas, 29, mechanic Chris Sherbert, 26, and bookkeeper Beverly Guy, 52, Ponder's mother, were found on the morning of November 6, 2003, and investigators said all four had been shot with the same pistol. NBC News reported that at his plea hearing Kohlhepp admitted shooting the workers after the shop's manager made him angry.

The next known killings came in December 2015. NPR, citing the arrest warrants, reported that Johnny Joe Coxie, 29, was shot on December 19, 2015, and that his wife, Meagan Leigh McCraw Coxie, 25, was kidnapped that day and shot on either December 20 or December 26. The couple had been hired to work on Kohlhepp's property and were reported missing in late December. Their remains were recovered in November 2016 after Kohlhepp led investigators to the graves.

The case broke open in 2016. Kala Brown, 30, and her boyfriend Charles David Carver, 32, disappeared on about August 31, 2016, after going to a cleaning job on Kohlhepp's fenced property of nearly 100 acres near Woodruff. The Associated Press reported that Spartanburg County deputies, led there by the couple's last known cellphone signals, found Brown chained inside a metal storage container on November 3, 2016, after about two months in captivity. Brown told investigators she had watched Kohlhepp shoot Carver, whose body was found in a shallow grave on the property the next day. Brown has spoken publicly about her ordeal.

Kohlhepp was arrested on November 3, 2016, and charged with kidnapping Brown. According to the AP, Sheriff Chuck Wright announced on November 5 that Kohlhepp had voluntarily confessed to the four Superbike murders and pointed out two more graves. On November 28, 2016, prosecutors added three murder counts for Carver and the Coxies with kidnapping and weapons charges, NBC News and NPR reported.

On May 26, 2017, Kohlhepp pleaded guilty in Spartanburg County to seven counts of murder, two counts of kidnapping, one count of first-degree criminal sexual conduct and weapons charges. WLOS reported that under the nine-page agreement, signed by Seventh Circuit Solicitor Barry Barnette, Sheriff Wright and Brown, he received seven consecutive life terms plus 30 years each for the kidnapping and sexual-conduct counts, waived his right to appeal, and agreed never to seek parole. Barnette said the state could have pursued execution but chose a plea in part because South Carolina's lethal-injection drugs had expired, NBC News reported. Through his attorney, Kohlhepp said there were no other victims.

That claim did not hold. The Associated Press reported in December 2017 that Kohlhepp had written an eight-page letter to the Spartanburg Herald-Journal saying he had additional undiscovered victims but saw no reason to give numbers or locations; the FBI's Columbia office confirmed a pending investigation. According to Wikipedia, he was named a person of interest in a 2003 Greer bank triple homicide, which he denied and which has not been linked to him. Brown and victims' relatives have filed civil suits.

Kohlhepp was born Todd Christopher Sampsell in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, on March 7, 1971, according to Wikipedia. As a teenager in Tempe, Arizona, he forced a 14-year-old neighbor into his home at gunpoint and assaulted her; the AP reported he pleaded guilty to kidnapping in 1987, the sexual-assault charge was dismissed, and he served about 15 years and had to register as a sex offender. After his release in 2001 he moved to South Carolina, obtained a real estate license in 2006 and built a brokerage with more than a dozen agents.

summary: Convicted of seven murders; died in prison in 2013. Walter Ellis strangled women on Milwaukee's north side between 1986 and 2007, was identified through a 2009 DNA review of unsolved homicides, and pleaded no contest in 2011.
narrative: Walter Ellis, known in Milwaukee as the North Side Strangler, was convicted of killing seven women in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, between 1986 and 2007. He was identified in 2009 after a police cold case review found that one DNA profile linked a series of unsolved homicides. In February 2011 he pleaded no contest to five counts of first-degree intentional homicide and two counts of first-degree murder, and Milwaukee County Circuit Judge Dennis Cimpl sentenced him to seven consecutive life sentences without parole. Ellis died on December 1, 2013, at age 53, while serving his sentence in South Dakota.

The seven charged homicides spanned 21 years. According to Associated Press reporting carried by CBS News, the victims were Deborah Harris and Tanya Miller, killed in October 1986; Florence McCormick, found dead in April 1995; Sheila Farrior, killed in 1995; Joyce Mims, killed in June 1997; and Ouithreaun Stokes, killed in April 2007. The seventh, Irene Smith, was killed in November 1992, according to the Wikipedia article on the case. All seven were strangled, by hand or with a rope or clothing, and one was also stabbed. Police said most were sex workers, which some families disputed.

In May 2009 the Milwaukee Police Department's cold case unit announced that DNA testing had linked seven unsolved deaths to a single unidentified man whose profile was in no database. CBS News reported that the unit sifted through thousands of cases and tested the DNA of more than 100 people. Police Chief Edward Flynn said investigators focused on Ellis after his name surfaced in several of the killings. Ellis was arrested on September 5, 2009, after police obtained his DNA; according to Wikipedia, officers seized a toothbrush from his apartment when he failed to appear for a court-ordered DNA collection, and he was taken into custody at a motel in Franklin, a Milwaukee suburb.

The Associated Press reported that his DNA matched semen from six victims and blood on a pepper spray can at the seventh scene. On September 10, 2009, District Attorney John Chisholm brought the charges to seven counts, and bond was set at one million dollars. Police said Ellis's DNA had in fact been matched to evidence from nine women, aged 16 to 41, though only seven deaths were charged.

The investigation exposed a failure in Wisconsin's DNA database. The Department of Corrections said it had taken a sample from Ellis in prison in 2001, but the state Justice Department said its crime laboratory never received it; authorities later said Ellis had persuaded a fellow inmate to submit a sample in his place. Chief Flynn said an earlier profile might have prevented at least one death, and the case prompted a full review of the state database.

Ellis first pleaded not guilty. On February 18, 2011, during a motion hearing, he unexpectedly entered no contest pleas, which carry a mandatory life sentence but do not admit guilt. Judge Cimpl, who could have allowed parole eligibility, declined and imposed seven consecutive life terms on February 24, 2011. The Wisconsin Supreme Court declined to hear his appeal in 2013, according to the Associated Press.

The DNA findings also unraveled two other convictions. FOX6 Milwaukee reported that Chaunte Ott and William Avery had each been convicted of a murder later linked to Ellis and were subsequently freed. According to Wikipedia, Ott served 14 years for the 1995 death of 16-year-old Jessica Payne before his 2009 release, and Avery was exonerated after Ellis's DNA was matched in 2010 to the 1998 killing of Maryetta Griffin. Ellis was never charged in either death.

Ellis was moved to South Dakota in June 2011 under an interstate compact and died in a Sioux Falls hospital on December 1, 2013, of what officials called natural causes; he never explained the killings. Born in Milwaukee on June 24, 1960, he left school after the eighth grade and, according to Wikipedia, built a record of robbery, theft, drug and assault offenses and served as a police informant in the 1990s.

victimProfile: Boys and young men aged 12 to 19, most of them hitchhikers picked up along Southern California freeways
captureMethod: Arrested on June 11, 1980, after Los Angeles police surveillance officers, acting on a tip from an acquaintance, followed his van and found him assaulting a teenage hitchhiker.

summary: Executed in 1996. William Bonin, the Freeway Killer, was convicted by juries in Los Angeles and Orange counties of murdering 14 boys and young men along Southern California freeways in 1979 and 1980; he confessed to 21.
narrative: William George Bonin, known as the Freeway Killer, was convicted of murdering 14 boys and young men in Southern California between August 1979 and June 1980. A Los Angeles County jury convicted him of 10 murders in January 1982 and an Orange County jury of four more in August 1983; he was sentenced to death in both cases. According to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation (CDCR), he was executed by lethal injection at San Quentin State Prison on February 23, 1996, the first California inmate put to death by that method. He had confessed to 21 killings to a television reporter, and investigators initially linked him to as many as 40 deaths.

The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals summarised the pattern in its 1995 opinion: Bonin picked up boys aged roughly 12 to 19, usually hitchhikers, sexually assaulted them inside his van, killed them, generally by strangulation, and left the bodies beside freeways. The victims of which he was convicted were Markus Grabs, Donald Hyden, David Murillo, Charles Miranda, James Macabe, Ronald Gatlin, Harry Turner, Steven Wood, Darin Kendrick and Steven Wells in Los Angeles County, and Dennis Frank Fox, Glenn Barker, Russell Rugh and Lawrence Sharp in Orange County. CDCR dates the first of these killings, of Grabs, to August 5, 1979, and the last, of Wells, to June 2, 1980.

Bonin did not always act alone. Vernon Butts, suspected in several of the killings, died by suicide in jail in January 1981 before trial. Gregory Miley and James Munro, both about 19 at the time, pleaded guilty to their roles in individual murders and testified against Bonin; the California Supreme Court's 1988 opinion recounts Miley's testimony about the killing of Charles Miranda and Munro's about the killing of Steven Wells. A fourth man, William Pugh, pleaded guilty to voluntary manslaughter and also testified.

According to the Wikipedia account, information Pugh gave to a counsellor pointed Los Angeles police to Bonin, a paroled sex offender. Officers placed him under surveillance and, on June 11, 1980, followed his van to a service station near the Hollywood Freeway, where they found him assaulting a teenage hitchhiker who survived. He was arrested at the scene. He later spoke with KNXT reporter David Lopez, who testified at both trials that Bonin admitted the killings; the California Supreme Court noted Lopez described admissions to 14 killings beyond the six at issue in Orange County.

The Los Angeles County trial began in November 1981. The Ninth Circuit noted that Bonin had been charged with 14 murders there; two counts were dismissed before trial and the jury acquitted him of two more. On January 6, 1982, the jury convicted him of 10 murders and 10 robberies, and Judge William Keene imposed death sentences on March 12, 1982. The Orange County trial opened in Santa Ana on June 14, 1983. United Press International reported that on August 2, 1983, after three days of deliberation, the jury found him guilty of the murders of Fox, Barker, Rugh and Sharp; CDCR records four further death sentences on August 26, 1983.

The California Supreme Court affirmed the Orange County judgment on August 29, 1988 (People v. Bonin, 46 Cal.3d 659), vacating three duplicate multiple-murder special-circumstance findings but leaving the death sentences intact, and affirmed the Los Angeles judgment on January 9, 1989. In federal court Bonin argued that his trial lawyer, William Charvet, had been compromised by a literary-rights deal and had failed to present evidence of childhood abuse and brain damage. On June 28, 1995, the Ninth Circuit rejected those claims (Bonin v. Calderon, 59 F.3d 815). Governor Pete Wilson denied clemency days before the execution. CDCR records that Bonin was pronounced dead at 12:13 a.m. on February 23, 1996.

Bonin was born on January 8, 1947, in Willimantic, Connecticut, and served in the U.S. Air Force in Vietnam before an honourable discharge in 1968. CDCR lists kidnapping and sex-offence charges from November 1968, which led to commitment to Atascadero State Hospital and then state prison, and a 1975 conviction for sexually assaulting a 14-year-old boy, for which he received one to 15 years. He was paroled in October 1978.
